Twelve words that every sleep scientist uses. Read the cards and say each word aloud. Which three do you already know?

circadian rhythmNOUN the body’s natural cycle of about 24 hoursNight shifts upset the circadian rhythm.
deprivationNOUN the state of not having something you need, e.g. sleepthe effects of sleep deprivation
consolidateVERB make something, e.g. a memory, stronger and more stableSleep consolidates new memories.
cognitiveADJ connected with thinking and learningcognitive performance
alertnessNOUN the state of being fully awake and quick to notice thingsCoffee increases alertness.
regulateVERB control a process so that it works at the right levelHormones regulate sleep.
disruptVERB interrupt something so that it cannot continue normallyNoise disrupts deep sleep.
chronicADJ lasting a long time or happening again and againa chronic lack of sleep
exposureNOUN the state of being in contact with something, e.g. lightexposure to bright light

3

Read like a detective

17 MIN

Before you read · 60-second survey. Look ONLY at the title, the headings and the first sentence of each section. Sections:   Why you forget after an all-nighter → section

The Night Shift: What the Brain Does While We Sleep

A textbook extract · about 630 words · B2–C1 · written for this book (from a fictional textbook)

1 · Introduction

AFor a long time, sleep was regarded as a passive state: a period in which the body simply switched off and waited for morning. This view has now been abandoned. Over the past few decades, sleep has been studied in laboratories around the world, and it is now understood as an active and highly organised process. This chapter is divided into four main parts. It first describes the stages of sleep and then explains how sleep is regulated by the body clock. Next, it examines the role of sleep in memory, and finally it considers what happens when sleep is lost.

2 · The stages of sleep

BSleep is not one single state. It is usually divided into two main types: non-rapid eye movement (non-REM) sleep and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. Non-REM sleep is further divided into lighter and deeper stages. During deep sleep, breathing slows, the heart rate falls and the sleeper is difficult to wake. This stage is often described as the most restorative, because it is associated with physical recovery and growth.

CREM sleep, by contrast, is a surprisingly active state. The eyes move quickly beneath the eyelids, brain activity resembles that of a waking person, and most vivid dreams are reported in this stage. Over a typical night, the sleeper moves through several cycles of non-REM and REM sleep, each lasting roughly an hour and a half.

3 · The body clock

DWhy do we feel sleepy at night and alert in the morning? The timing of sleep is controlled largely by the circadian rhythm, an internal cycle of about twenty-four hours. This rhythm is regulated by a small area of the brain which responds to light received through the eyes. When it gets dark, a hormone called melatonin is released, and the body is prepared for sleep. Exposure to bright light in the evening, including light from phones and laptops, can delay this process.

EThe body clock also changes with age. In adolescence, the rhythm tends to shift later, so many young people do not feel sleepy until late at night. Many university students, in Navoi as much as in Seoul or London, go to bed long after midnight and then struggle through morning lectures. Their bodies are simply not ready for an early start.

4 · Sleep and memory

FOne of the most important discoveries of sleep research is that sleep supports learning. During the day, new information is stored only temporarily. During sleep, and especially during deep sleep, many of these memories appear to be replayed and consolidated, so that they become more stable and easier to recall. It has also been suggested that sleep helps the brain to connect new information with what is already known. For students, the message is clear: a night of sleep after studying is not wasted time, but part of the learning process itself.

5 · The cost of lost sleep

GSleep deprivation affects almost every aspect of cognitive performance. After a night without sleep, attention and reaction time are impaired, and mistakes become more frequent. Mood suffers too: tired people are often more irritable and anxious. When sleep is cut short night after night, the problem becomes chronic. Long-term sleep loss has been linked to a range of health problems, including weaker immunity and a higher risk of heart disease. Most health organisations recommend that adults sleep about seven to nine hours a night, although individual needs vary.

6 · Conclusion

HIn short, sleep is not a pause in life but a period of intense biological work. While we sleep, the brain organises memories, the body recovers and the internal clock is reset for the next day. Many questions, however, remain unanswered. Scientists still do not fully understand why we dream, or exactly how much sleep different people need. What is already clear is that sleep should be treated as a basic need, as important for success at university as attendance or hard work.

Read only the first sentence of each section. Do you already know the whole story?

Language toolkit: the academic passive

10 MIN

Academic texts are full of passive verbs. The passive puts the process or the result at the front of the sentence, and the people who did it in the background.

Notice find it

Find these sentences in the chapter and complete them.

1. (A) For a long time, sleep as a passive state.

2. (A) This chapter into four main parts.

3. (A) Over the past few decades, sleep in laboratories around the world.

4. (D) When it gets dark, a hormone called melatonin .

5. (F) It that sleep helps the brain to connect new information …

6. (H) … sleep as a basic need.

The rule rule
TenseForm: be + past participleExample from the chapter
Present simpleam / is / are + V3Sleep is divided into two main types.
Past simplewas / were + V3Sleep was regarded as a passive state.
Present perfecthas / have been + V3Sleep has been studied in laboratories.
Modalmodal + be + V3Sleep should be treated as a basic need.
“It” + passiveIt is / has been + V3 + that …It has been suggested that sleep helps …

Three rules

  • be + past participle: is divided ✓  ·  is divide ✗  ·  has been shown ✓  ·  has been show ✗
  • No passive for happen, occur, arrive: Dreams are happened ✗ → Dreams happen ✓
  • Add “by …” only when the doer is new or important: Melatonin is released (by the body). · The rhythm is regulated by a small area of the brain.
Fix it correct
Broken sentenceFixed sentence
1. Sleep is divide into several stages.
2. Melatonin is produce when it gets dark.
3. Many experiments have been make on sleep.
4. Most dreams are happened in REM sleep.
5. It has been show that sleep helps memory.
☆Make it academic write

Rewrite in the passive. Leave out the doer if it is not important.

a) Researchers measure brain activity during sleep. →

b) Bright screens can delay the release of melatonin. →

c) Universities should start morning lectures later. →

Level up: report what a text does

CONTINUED

At B2 you say what a text is about. At C1 you say what it does — and you notice when the writer is careful.

ToolPhrasesExample
Reporting verbs
say what the writer does		outlines · examines · considers · argues · concludesSection 2 outlines the two main types of sleep.
Nominalisation
a section in one noun		regulate → the regulation of · lose sleep → sleep loss · recover → recoverySection 3 deals with the regulation of sleep by the body clock.
Sequencing a structure
guide the reader		It opens with … · This is followed by … · The subsequent section turns to … · It concludes by …The chapter opens with an overview. This is followed by a section on sleep stages.
Academic hedging
how sure is the writer?		appear to · tend to · it has been suggested that · has been linked toMemories appear to be replayed during sleep. (= likely, not proven)

The scholar’s tool: the city map

10 MIN

Before a scholar rode into Merv, he studied a map: where the gate was, which streets led to the library, where to leave the city. An academic text is a city too. Surveying it for two minutes before you read saves you twenty minutes of getting lost.

Survey the whole text; then read closely only the sections that answer your question.

On the mapIn the textWhat it tells youWhen to read
City gateTitle (+ subtitle)the topic and often the writer’s anglealways first
Notice boardIntroduction: the plan“This chapter is divided into …”always
StreetsSection headingswhat each part of the text is aboutin the survey
SignpostsTopic sentencesthe main point of each paragraphin the survey
HousesDetails: evidence, examples, numbersthe proof behind each main pointonly when you need them
Exit gateConclusionthe summary + what is still unknownalways

Tool tips: It is often claimed that … · It has been shown that … · … is linked to … · … is delayed by … · … is not yet fully understood.

Phrase bank: describing a text’s structure use these
JobB2 · safeC1 · upgrade
City gate · name the textThe chapter is entitled “…”. · It deals with …The chapter, entitled “…”, examines … · It provides an overview of …
Notice board · give the planThe text is divided into … sections. · It consists of …The text falls into … main parts. · It is organised around …
Streets · walk the sectionsSection 2 describes … · This is followed by …It opens with … · The subsequent section turns to … · Section 4 outlines …
Exit gate · the main ideaThe key point is that … · The final section sums up …The overarching argument is that … · The chapter concludes by …

Common traps

✗ The text is divided on six parts.
✓ The text is divided into six parts.
✗ The chapter consists from six sections.
✓ The chapter consists of six sections.
✗ In this text is written about sleep.
✓ This text deals with sleep.
✗ Most dreams are happened in REM sleep.
✓ Most dreams happen in REM sleep.

Be the examiner

7 MIN

Examiners use four criteria. Learn them by marking someone else’s work first — then use them on your own structure description in Level 3.

CriterionA C1 structure description …
T · Taskanswers the exact task and keeps one clear route from the city gate to the exit gate
O · Organisationhas one idea per sentence (title · plan · sections · conclusion) and links ideas with more than First / Then
V · Vocabularyuses precise topic words and collocations in an academic tone
G · Grammaruses a range of structures with few errors; in this stop: the academic passive (is divided into, has been studied, It has been suggested that …)

Score each criterion: 1 = not yet · 2 = almost · 3 = yes

Two students described the structure of the nap-room report from Watch a scholar survey a text. Mark both.

Student A
This report is about nap rooms at universities. It is divide into five sections. First, it gives some background about rest rooms at other universities. Then it talks about how students sleep in term time. After that, the good and bad sides of naps are discuss. In the last section is recommended to open a nap room for one semester as a trial.
Student B
The report, entitled “Should Universities Provide Nap Rooms?”, falls into five short sections. It opens with background on rest rooms at other universities and then outlines students’ sleep habits in term time. This is followed by an assessment of the benefits and risks of daytime naps. The final section recommends opening a nap room for one semester as a trial.

Which criterion shows the biggest difference between A and B? Why?

Try the bank (model): The chapter, entitled “The Night Shift”, examines what the brain does during sleep. It falls into six sections: it opens with an introduction, which is followed by sections on the stages of sleep, the body clock, memory and the cost of lost sleep. The final section sums up and lists open questions.

7 · Levels 1–2

Read like a detective

17 MIN

Before you read · use last stop’s map. Survey the title and headings for 60 seconds. What is the biggest threat, according to the headings?

A Warmer Century: Climate Change and Central Asia

An article from an academic magazine · about 500 words · B2–C1 · written for this book

Introduction

AClimate change is no longer a distant forecast. Over the past century, the average temperature of the Earth’s surface has risen noticeably, and most scientists agree that human activity, above all the burning of fossil fuels, has been the main cause. Coal, oil and gas release carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases, which trap heat in the atmosphere. This article argues that, although climate change is a global process, its effects are felt locally, and Central Asia is one of the regions where they have already become visible.

A warming region

BCentral Asia has become noticeably warmer in recent decades. Summers in cities such as Tashkent, Bukhara and Navoi have grown longer and hotter, and heatwaves have become more frequent. Some regional studies suggest that the region is warming at least as fast as the global average. For many older residents, the change is not a matter of statistics: they remember snowy winters that their grandchildren have never seen.

Shrinking glaciers, uncertain rivers

CThe most serious threat, however, concerns water. The two great rivers of the region, the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya, are fed largely by snow and ice from the Pamir and Tian Shan mountains. Many of these glaciers have shrunk considerably, and scientists have warned that the loss will continue. In the short term, faster melting may even increase the flow of some rivers. In the long term, however, there will be less ice to melt, and summer water supplies may fall just when they are needed most.

DWater has always been precious in Central Asia. The loss of much of the Aral Sea, which was caused mainly by large-scale irrigation in the twentieth century rather than by climate change, has shown how quickly a water crisis can damage health, farming and whole communities. A warmer climate could make similar mistakes even more costly.

Farming under pressure

EAgriculture is particularly vulnerable. Crops such as cotton and wheat depend on irrigation, and higher temperatures increase the amount of water that plants and soil lose. Droughts have become a serious concern for farmers in several parts of the region. Some farmers have already switched to drip irrigation, which delivers water directly to the roots, or to crops that need less water.

Two responses: mitigation and adaptation

FExperts usually divide the response to climate change into two kinds. Mitigation means reducing emissions so that warming slows down; adaptation means preparing for the changes that can no longer be avoided. Central Asia needs both. Uzbekistan, for example, has built large solar power plants, including one near Navoi, which reduce the need for fossil fuels. At the same time, many towns have started planting trees to provide shade, and water is being used more carefully.

Conclusion

GThe evidence is clear: the climate of Central Asia has already changed, and water is where the change will be felt most. The consequences, however, are not fixed. Whether the region suffers or adapts will depend on decisions taken in the next few decades by governments, by farmers and by ordinary citizens who choose how to use energy and water every day.

Find the sentence in A that begins “This article argues …”. That is the writer’s main claim.
Jigsaw option. Group A sieves paragraphs A–B, Group B C–D, Group C E–G. Agree on ONE main point per paragraph (max. 12 words), then build the list for the whole article in mixed groups.
Talk after reading: Which consequence in the article worries you most? Is there anything the article left out that matters in your region?

Toolkit: the present perfect for trends

Scientists use the present perfect for a change from the past up to now and for findings that still matter.

Notice find it

The rule rule
UseForm + time wordsExample
A trend up to nowhas / have + V3 · over the past …, in recent decades, since …Temperatures have risen over the past century.
A research findingResearchers / Studies + have + found / shown / warnedScientists have warned that the loss will continue.
A result nowhas / have + already / now + V3Some farmers have already switched to drip irrigation.
Finished time → past simpleV2 · in 1990, in the 20th century, agoMuch of the Aral Sea disappeared in the twentieth century.

Three rules

  • One thing → has: The temperature has risen. · The number of droughts has grown.
  • since + a point, for + a period: since 1990 · for thirty years · over the past thirty years
  • Learn the V3: risen · grown · shrunk · fallen · become · found · shown

Level up: C1 reporting tools

CONTINUED

At C1 a summary does not only repeat what a text says. It shows what the writer does (argues, warns, admits), reports how sure the writer is, and packs each point into as few words as possible.

ToolPhrasesExample
Reporting verbs
show what the writer does		argues · contends · warns · acknowledges · concludesThe writer warns that summer water supplies may fall.
Nominalisation
verb or adjective → noun		shrink → the shrinking of · lose → loss · vulnerable → vulnerabilityGlaciers are shrinking. → The shrinking of glaciers threatens river flow.
Cautious reporting
keep the writer’s certainty		suggests · indicates · is likely to · appears toRegional studies suggest that the region is warming fast.
Condensing
two points, one sentence		not only … but also · , which … · , arguing that …The article examines the region’s warming, arguing that water is most at risk.

The Climate on Our Plate · a short magazine text written for this book
Food waste has become a climate problem. When food is thrown away, all the water, land and energy that were used to grow, transport and cook it are wasted too. Food that rots in landfill also releases methane, a powerful greenhouse gas. In many homes, bread, fruit and cooked rice are among the things most often thrown away. Fortunately, the problem is easy to reduce. Many Uzbek families still follow the old rule that bread must never be thrown away, and experts suggest similar small steps: planning meals, storing food correctly and using leftovers creatively. Researchers have found that such small changes, repeated in millions of homes, can add up to a large effect.

Be the examiner

7 MIN

Examiners use four criteria. Learn them by marking someone else’s work first — then use them on your own summary.

CriterionA C1 summary …
T · Taskanswers the exact question and keeps one clear position — the writer’s — from the rim to the bowl
O · Organisationhas one idea per sentence (source → main points → kept detail → message) and links ideas with more than Firstly / Secondly
V · Vocabularyuses precise topic words and collocations in an academic tone
G · Grammaruses a range of structures with few errors; in this stop: the present perfect for trends and findings (have risen, Studies have shown; past simple for finished time)

Score each criterion: 1 = not yet · 2 = almost · 3 = yes

In my opinion, the government must give them money.

The shrinking of the Pamir and Tian Shan glaciers is likely to reduce summer river flow in the long term, even if faster melting may briefly increase it. The writer also highlights the vulnerability of irrigated farming, since heat increases water loss, and notes that some farmers have already adapted.

Read like a detective

17 MIN

Before you read · map + sieve. Survey the title and headings. Which section will help you most to find what an advert hides? Section

Selling a Feeling: The Language of Persuasion in Advertising

A textbook extract · about 530 words · B2–C1 · written for this book (from Introduction to Media Studies, a fictional textbook)

1 · Introduction

APersuasion is as old as the bazaar. Long before television, traders in Bukhara and Samarkand called out to passers-by, praised the quality of their silk and promised the lowest price in the market. Modern advertising follows the same principle, but with far greater resources: careful research into consumers, professional design and the ability to reach millions of people at once. This chapter examines the main techniques of persuasion in advertising and explains why the critical reading of adverts is an essential skill.

2 · Knowing the audience

BEvery successful advert begins with a clear target audience. Before a campaign is launched, advertisers collect information about the age, income, interests and values of potential buyers. The selection of images, music and language depends on this analysis. An advert for a sports drink aimed at teenagers, for example, will rely on energy, humour and speed, whereas an advert for a bank aimed at families will emphasise security and trust.

3 · Three classic appeals

CMany techniques used today can be traced back to the three forms of persuasion described by the Greek philosopher Aristotle. An appeal to credibility (ethos) relies on the authority of the speaker, such as a doctor in a white coat or a famous athlete. An appeal to emotion (pathos) creates feelings of happiness, fear or belonging. An appeal to logic (logos) presents facts, numbers and comparisons. Most adverts combine all three, but emotional appeals are often the most powerful, because buying decisions are rarely made by reason alone.

4 · Words that sell

DThe language of advertising is short, positive and memorable. Slogans are built on repetition, rhyme and direct address (“you”), and imperatives such as “Try it today” or “Discover the difference” invite immediate action. Advertisers also make frequent use of so-called weasel words: expressions such as “helps to”, “up to” or “virtually” that sound like strong promises but in fact promise very little. A shampoo that “helps to reduce” hair loss does not claim to stop it.

5 · Pictures that persuade

EVisual elements often communicate more than the text. The choice of colour creates associations: green suggests nature and health, while gold suggests luxury. Smiling faces encourage identification with the people in the advert, and celebrity endorsements transfer the popularity of a star to the product. Even the position of a product in the picture is carefully planned, since the eye is usually drawn to the centre and to faces.

6 · What the advert does not say

FPerhaps the most important feature of an advert is what it leaves out. Adverts present only the advantages of a product; risks, costs and limitations are hidden in small print or omitted entirely. This bias is not necessarily dishonest, since an advert is not a scientific report, but it means that the reader receives a one-sided picture. Statistics may also be misleading: “nine out of ten users” means little if we do not know how many users were asked.

7 · Conclusion

GAdvertising is not simply a source of information; it is a carefully designed act of persuasion. The recognition of its techniques does not make us immune, but it does allow us to make more independent decisions. For students, the analysis of adverts offers a further benefit: it trains the same critical reading skills that are needed for academic texts.

LEVEL 2

Pack a new text

Reading the Small Print · a short textbook text · about 125 words · written for this book
Many adverts carry two messages. The large text makes a promise; the small print, placed at the bottom of a poster or shown for a second at the end of a video, sets the conditions. A “free” trial may turn into a monthly payment, a discount may apply only to selected products, and a guarantee may depend on daily use. Small print is not always dishonest: some details must be included for legal reasons, and a poster has little space. However, its size and position make it easy to ignore. A careful reader therefore looks for three things before buying: the full price, the length of any contract and the conditions behind every guarantee. In short, the most important information is often the least visible.

Read like a detective

17 MIN

Before you read (two texts · about 610 words in all): Text 1 is a textbook extract. Text 2 is a follow-up report on the same topic. What will Text 2 probably do? Tick one.   repeat Text 1   add to it or question it   change the topic

Why Do Some Innovations Spread?

Text 1 · A textbook extract written for this book · about 400 words · B2–C1

1 · Invention is not innovation

AIn everyday speech, the words invention and innovation are often used as if they meant the same thing. Scholars, however, tend to separate them. An invention is a new idea or device; an innovation is an invention that people actually adopt and use. Many inventions never become innovations. They remain prototypes in a laboratory or drawings in a notebook, because nobody finds a reason to use them.

2 · What makes people adopt something new?

BResearchers who study the diffusion of new technologies have identified several features that appear to make adoption more likely. The first is a clear advantage: people are more likely to change their habits when a new product is noticeably cheaper, faster or safer than the old one. The second is compatibility. An innovation that fits existing values and routines tends to spread more easily than one that asks people to change their whole way of life.

CSimplicity also seems to matter. If a new tool is difficult to understand, people may give up before they see its benefits. Finally, people are often more willing to try something new when they can test it on a small scale, or when they can see that their neighbours are already using it successfully. In many communities, a trusted neighbour may be more persuasive than any advertisement.

3 · Old roads, new ideas

DThese features are not new. Historians generally agree that paper-making reached the Islamic world through Central Asia, and Samarkand became famous for its paper. Paper was cheaper and lighter than parchment, it suited the needs of scribes and merchants, and its advantages could be seen on every market table. It is likely that the trade routes themselves acted as a kind of network, carrying ideas as well as goods.

4 · Doing more with less

EIn recent decades, attention has turned to frugal innovation: designing products that are simple, affordable and strong enough for people with limited resources. Examples that are often discussed include low-cost medical devices, solar lamps for villages without a reliable electricity supply and mobile phone services that allow people without a bank account to send money. Some writers argue that such innovations could eventually move from poorer markets to richer ones, reversing the usual direction of diffusion.

FFrugal innovation is undoubtedly an attractive idea. A cheaper product that does the same job benefits everyone: the user saves money, the producer reaches new customers and fewer resources are wasted. For this reason, frugal innovation is clearly the solution to the problem of inequality.

Find two words that show the writer is VERY sure. Where are they?
Öqiş va yozuv amaliyotiModule 3 · Practical class 19
3

The follow-up: a second look

CONTINUED

A follow-up reading checks a claim in a second source: does it agree, extend or challenge it?

Frugal Innovation: A Second Look

Text 2 · A short follow-up report written for this book · about 210 words · B2–C1

GThe textbook chapter presents frugal innovation in largely positive terms. A closer look at the research, however, suggests a more mixed picture.

HFirst, much of the evidence comes from case studies of individual products that succeeded. Failures are rarely written about, so the overall success rate is likely to be lower than the famous examples imply.

ISecond, a low price does not automatically mean that a product reaches the people who need it most. In remote areas, delivery, repair and training may cost more than the product itself. A solar lamp that cannot be repaired locally might be used for a year and then abandoned.

JThird, it is not entirely clear who benefits most. In some cases, the main winners appear to be large companies that open new markets, rather than the communities that the products were designed for.

KNone of this means that frugal innovation is a mistake. It does, however, indicate that a cheap product is only one part of a solution. Its success seems to depend on the same conditions that the textbook describes for every innovation: trust, compatibility with local life and visible results. Readers may therefore wish to treat the claim that frugal innovation is “clearly the solution to inequality” with some caution.

Text 2 never says “Text 1 is wrong”. How does it disagree, then?
Jigsaw option. Group A: Text 1, sections 1–2 · Group B: Text 1, sections 3–4 · Group C: Text 2. Agree on your main claim and how sure the writer is; teach it to a mixed group in 60 seconds.
Talk after reading: Which text do you trust more on frugal innovation? Give one reason from each text.

Language toolkit: hedging

10 MIN

Hedging shows how sure you are: a hedge softens a claim (may), a booster strengthens it (clearly).

Notice find it

3. (C) Simplicity also matter.

The certainty dial rule
How sure?LanguageExample from the texts
🔊 certainclearly · undoubtedly · it is clear that… is undoubtedly an attractive idea.
🔉 likelybe likely to · probably · tend toThe success rate is likely to be lower.
🔈 possiblemay · might · could · appear to · seem toSimplicity also seems to matter.
📄 evidencesuggest · indicate · implyThe research suggests …
🎚 softenerssome · many · often · in some casesIn some cases, the main winners …

Three rules

  • Hedge claims, not facts: Paper is lighter than parchment ✓  ·  Paper may be lighter … ✗
  • One hedge is enough: It might possibly perhaps suggest … ✗  ·  It might suggest … ✓
  • Watch the grammar: tend / appear / seem / be likely to + base verb · it is likely that + clause

The scholar’s tool: the astrolabe

10 MIN

Astronomers of the Islamic world — including the scholars of Samarkand — used the astrolabe to measure how high a star stood above the horizon. A careful reader uses one to measure how high a claim stands: certain, likely, possible or doubtful. Then she looks at the same star from a second place: the follow-up text.

When two texts measure the same claim differently, compare their evidence.

Task: Compare how Text 1 and Text 2 present frugal innovation. Which text is more convincing? Bahodir (a fictional student) read both texts with his astrolabe and wrote this short comparison.
Topic
(1) Text 1 and Text 2 both discuss frugal innovation, but they measure its value very differently.
Text 1 says
(2) Text 1, a textbook extract, argues that cheap and simple products benefit users, producers and the environment. (3) Its final claim is very strong: frugal innovation is “clearly the solution to the problem of inequality”.
Text 2 replies

(7) On balance, Text 2 appears to be more convincing, because its claims match its evidence. (8) Text 1 may be right that frugal products can help, but it seems to overstate how much they can achieve on their own.

7 · The ladder

Level 1: tend to · compatible with their routines · accepts / supports · may · the product itself · suggest · only one part of a solution.
Level 2: 1 4 (plain fact) → A (“most of the 200 families”) · 2 4 clearly → C (only “fewer cases”; no records from before) · 3 2 may → N · 4 4 undoubtedly → C (cracked filters; long-term use depends on repair). Report (e.g.): Text A is very sure (“clearly”, “undoubtedly”). Text B agrees that the filters appear to help but qualifies the strong claims: there are no earlier records, and cracked filters suggest that long-term use is likely to depend on repair. Text B seems more reliable.
Level 3: open (a real article); check the reference details, three measured claims with the authors’ own words, and a verdict on evidence.

3

Read like a detective

17 MIN

Before you read: look at the title and the headings. The writer will probably argue that resilience is …   a gift   more than a gift   a myth

Rethinking Resilience: Trait, Process or Community?

An academic article written for this book · about 530 words · B2–C1

Introduction

AWhen a student fails an exam and tries again, or a family rebuilds its home after a flood, we often say that they are resilient. In everyday speech, the word usually describes a personal quality: some people, it seems, are simply tough. This article argues that this popular view is incomplete. Resilience is better understood as a process that depends not only on the individual, but also on the people and conditions around them.

The popular view: a personal trait

BFirstly, it is worth asking why the trait view is so attractive. Films and social media are full of stories about individuals who overcame terrible adversity through willpower alone. Popular self-help books often make a similar promise. Such stories are inspiring, and they carry a hopeful message: if strength comes from inside, then anyone can decide to be strong.

Ordinary, not heroic

CHowever, research over the past few decades points in a different direction. Many studies suggest that most people who experience serious adversity — illness, the loss of a loved one, even a natural disaster — eventually return to normal life. This suggests that resilience is not a rare gift possessed by a few heroes, but a common human capacity. It is ordinary rather than extraordinary.

DFurthermore, resilience appears to change over time and from one situation to another. A student who copes well with exam pressure may struggle after moving to a new city, and a person who felt helpless at twenty may be remarkably strong at forty. In other words, resilience is less like eye colour, which we cannot change, and more like physical fitness: it can grow, and it can weaken.

The power of relationships

EPerhaps the most consistent finding in resilience research is the importance of relationships. People with a strong support network tend to recover from setbacks more quickly than those who face them alone. In Uzbekistan, for example, the mahalla has traditionally offered such a network: when a family faces difficulty, neighbours often help with food, money or simply company. As a result, the burden is shared, and no one has to carry it alone.

Circle every word that tells you the writer is about to TURN.
While you read: write N in the margin next to the writer’s position, T next to every turn and R next to every result. You will need these marks for the case files.
Read the headings first: “An objection” (F) shows where the writer turns to the other side.
Öqiş va yozuv amaliyotiModule 3 · Practical class 20
3

Read like a detective

CONTINUED

An objection

FCritics might object that this view removes personal responsibility. Admittedly, individual effort matters: people who persevere, plan ahead and use healthy coping strategies generally do better. Nevertheless, focusing only on the individual can be harmful. If resilience is seen purely as personal strength, those who struggle may blame themselves, and decision-makers may conclude that support services are unnecessary.

What universities can do

GFor universities, this argument has practical consequences. Rather than simply telling students to “be strong”, institutions could build environments that support resilience: mentoring for first-year students, counselling that is easy to reach, and study groups that turn strangers into a support network. Such measures are likely to help vulnerable students most. Even a small step, such as an older student who checks on a newcomer during the first difficult weeks, may matter more than a single motivational lecture.

Conclusion

HIn sum, resilience is not a fixed trait that a lucky few are born with. It is a process that grows from the interaction between a person and their surroundings. Therefore, the most useful question is not “Is this person resilient?” but “What helps people to recover — and how can we provide it?”

Jigsaw option. Group A: paragraphs A–B · Group B: C–D · Group C: E–F · Group D: G–H. Find your signposts and say in one sentence which way your part moves the argument. Then teach it to a mixed group in 60 seconds.
Talk after reading: Which turn in the argument surprised you most? Do you agree with the writer’s conclusion in H? Why / why not?

Read the compass rule
DirectionSignpostsFrom the article
East · addFurthermore · Moreover · In addition · AlsoFurthermore, resilience …
West · turnHowever · Nevertheless · On the other handHowever, research …
South · resultAs a result · Therefore · This suggests thatAs a result, the burden …
Round · say againIn other words · That is to say · Put simplyIn other words, …
Stop · exampleFor example · For instance · such as…, for example, the mahalla …
Order · endFirstly · Finally · In sum · To concludeIn sum, resilience …

Three rules

  • Comma after a signpost at the start: However, … · As a result, … · In other words, …
  • However is not “but”: I was tired, however I studied. ✗ → I was tired. However, I studied. ✓
  • As a result + clause · as a result of + noun: As a result of the support, she recovered. ✓

LEVEL 2

Read the needle

Let Students Fail — a Little · An opinion piece · written for this book · about 150 words
Many universities try to protect first-year students from failure. I would argue that this kindness may do more harm than good, because small, safe failures are one of the best ways to build resilience. Firstly, a student who fails a practice test learns that a setback is not the end of the world. Furthermore, early failures show students where they need help while there is still time to get it. A weak first essay, for example, can send a student to a writing tutor in October rather than in May. Admittedly, failure is painful, and a student who fails again and again may lose confidence. However, the answer is not to remove failure but to make it safe: low-stakes tests, clear feedback and a mentor to talk to. Therefore, universities should not ask how to stop students failing, but how to help them fail early, fail small and recover.

Examiners use four criteria. Learn them by marking someone else’s work first — then use them on your own summary.

CriterionA C1 summary of an argument …
T · Taskreports the writer’s position and every turn accurately, from north to south, and keeps the reader’s own opinion out

V · Vocabularyuses precise topic words and collocations in an academic tone

Independent study · MT7 · a reflective essay

Step 1 (this page) is your preparation: the map and summary of a real article. Step 2: write a 300–350-word reflective essay about overcoming a difficulty, your own or that of a well-known real person. Read the experience through the article from Step 1 and cite it at least once (APA 7: in the text and in a reference at the end), as Kamola does in a short form in Walk with the compass. Marked out of 100: relevance of the reflection 40 · logical coherence 30 · link to the source 30.

2 · Word Bazaar

Dominoes: face adversity · cope with stress · suffer a setback · bounce back quickly · build resilience · rely on a support network.
Odd one out: 1 achievement (a success; the others are problems) · 2 surrender (giving up; the others deal with a problem) · 3 situation (outside a person; the others are qualities).

3 · Reading and case files

Before you read: more than a gift.
Case 1: A iv · B ii · C vii · D x · E v · F i · G vi · H ix (iii and viii are extra).
☆ Case 2: 1 F · 2 T · 3 NG · 4 T · 5 F · 6 NG.

Case 4: 1 A · 2 C.
Case 5: 1 A · 2 B · 3 remarkably.
Case 6 (any three): Firstly (B, order) · Admittedly (F, a step to the other side) · Rather than (G, contrast) · such as (G, example) · In sum (H, end).

4 · Signposting

Notice: 1 However · 2 suggests · 3 Furthermore · 4 other · 5 result · 6 Nevertheless.
Fix it: 1 I failed my first test. However, I did not give up. · 2 On the other hand, … · 3 Because she asked for help, she passed. · 4 … Nevertheless, she kept studying. · 5 Finally / To conclude, friends are important. · 6 For example, the mahalla … · 7 As a result, the burden … · 8 He was nervous. Nevertheless, he gave his talk. · 9 Despite the setback (In spite of the setback), …

4 · Level up

☆ Notice (any four): This article argues that (A) · it is worth asking (B) · Critics might object that (F) · Admittedly (F) · Nevertheless (F) · In sum (H) · Therefore (H).
☆ Make it C1 (model answers): 1 The writer concedes that effort matters but goes on to argue that support matters more. · 2 In retrospect, I was lonely rather than weak. · 3 My recovery began with the realisation that I needed help. · 4 This may explain why I coped better in my second year. · 5 My isolation in a new city made my first month hard.

5 · Compass and model

Turn: the second sentence (Nevertheless, …).
Route map: E Perhaps … · As a result — add (strongest support): support networks speed recovery · F Admittedly · Nevertheless — turn and back: objection, then reply · G Rather than — result: universities should build support · H In sum · Therefore — north again: resilience is a process.
☆ 1 However, At first, This suggests, As a result, In other words (also Next time); the turn is However · 2 sentence 4 · 3 sentence 7 · 4 In other words · ☆ 5 open.

6 · Academic takes (model answers)

Failure is not always caused by a lack of effort; support and circumstances also play a role. · A positive attitude may help, but recovery also tends to depend on other people. · No method can remove stress completely; however, some coping strategies can reduce it. · Pain is not always a sign of progress: ignoring an injury can lead to a second one. · ☆ Adapting to university can be hard even for able students; however, support tends to help.

7 · The ladder

Level 1: process · the individual and the people and conditions around them · eventually return to normal life · changes · a strong support network · individual effort matters · focusing only on the individual can be harmful · What helps people to recover — and how can we provide it?
Level 2: Claim (I would argue that): small, safe failures build resilience · Reason 1 (Firstly): a setback is not the end · Reason 2 (Furthermore, for example): early failures show where help is needed · Concession (Admittedly): failure hurts · Rebuttal (However): make failure safe · Conclusion (Therefore): fail early, fail small, recover. Summary and Level 3: open.
MT7: a reflective essay (300–350 words) that cites the Step 1 article; a full model is in the Teacher’s Guide.

Student A: T 1 · O 2 · V 2 · G 2 (T: no objection or reply from F, own opinion at the end; O: a list with no turn; V: very important, repeated verbs; G: says about, At last). Student B: 3 · 3 · 3 · 3. The biggest difference is in T (2 points).
☆ Be the editor (e.g.): The writer concedes that individual effort matters; nevertheless, … · Finally, the writer concludes that …
☆ Fix the summary: 1 discusses · 2 … matters. However, … / …, but … · 3 Because most people recover, … · 4 Finally, …

3

Read like a detective

17 MIN

Before you read: look at the headings only. Where will the writer give their own verdict?   at the start   in every paragraph   near the end

Connected but Divided? Social Media and Public Life

A discursive article written for this book · about 530 words · B2–C1

Introduction

AWithin a single generation, social media has moved from the edges of public life to its centre. For many young people, platforms are where they first hear the news, follow debates and form opinions. Supporters see a powerful tool for democracy; critics see a machine that divides societies. Few technologies have provoked such strong feelings so quickly. This article examines both views before offering a judgement.

The case for: a louder public voice

BOn the positive side, social media has given a voice to people who were rarely heard before. Anyone with a phone can report an event, start a campaign or question a public official. Granted that not every post is accurate, the sheer number of voices makes it harder for any single institution to control what the public knows.

CSupporters also point to civic benefits. Volunteers use online groups to organise help after floods or earthquakes, and local communities use messaging channels to share practical information quickly. Small businesses, from family bakeries to young designers, can reach customers without paying for expensive advertising. In Uzbekistan, for instance, many universities and mahallas now post announcements on Telegram channels. For such groups, social media is less a battlefield than a noticeboard.

The case against: echo chambers and outrage

DCritics, however, argue that the same tools can damage public debate. Because algorithms tend to show users content similar to what they have liked before, people may end up in echo chambers, rarely meeting views that challenge their own. Over time, this could contribute to polarisation, as each group becomes more certain that the other side is not only wrong but dangerous. Some observers also worry that people now spend so much time arguing with strangers online that they talk less with the neighbours who disagree with them.

EA second concern is the speed of misinformation. Posts that provoke outrage often receive more engagement than calm, accurate ones, and platforms may therefore amplify them. Admittedly, false rumours existed long before the internet; nevertheless, they have never travelled so far, so fast. Corrections, when they finally appear, rarely travel as far as the original false claim.

Who is speaking in each paragraph: a supporter, a critic or the judge?
While you read: write 1 (Side 1: for) or 2 (Side 2: against) in the margin next to each argument, and draw a small step ⤳ wherever the writer admits that the other side has a point.
Separate reported views from the writer’s own view: B–E report what supporters and critics say; only F–H give the writer’s judgement.
Öqiş va yozuv amaliyotiModule 3 · Practical class 21
3

Read like a detective

CONTINUED

Weighing the evidence

FWhich side has the stronger case? While both sides make valid points, the evidence is more mixed than either of them suggests. Some researchers have found that many users actually meet a wider range of views online than offline, which challenges the simple echo-chamber story. On the other hand, the problem of misinformation appears to be real, especially during emergencies, when people need reliable information most.

GIt is also worth noting that the effects of social media depend heavily on how it is used — and by whom. A well-informed user with strong digital literacy can use platforms to learn from many sources; a less careful user may simply absorb whatever the algorithm offers. In this sense, the question is less about technology than about education: the same platform can be a library or a rumour mill.

Conclusion

HOn balance, social media is neither the saviour nor the destroyer of public life. Admittedly, it has created new risks. However, banning it or ignoring it is unrealistic. A more promising response is to combine sensible regulation of the largest platforms with education in digital literacy, so that citizens can enjoy the benefits while recognising the dangers.

Jigsaw option. Group A: the case for (B–C) · Group B: the case against (D–E) · Group C: the judge (F–H). Each group presents its part in 60 seconds — as a lawyer or, for Group C, as the judge.
Talk after reading: Is the writer really neutral? Which side gets more space — and which side gets the last word?

Language toolkit: concession

10 MIN

Concession = admit that the other side has a point, then come back to your own view.

Notice find it

Find these sentences in the article and complete them.

1. (B) that not every post is accurate, the sheer number of voices makes it harder …

2. (E) , false rumours existed long before the internet; , they have never travelled so far …

3. (F) both sides make valid points, the evidence is more mixed …

4. (H) , it has created new risks. , banning it or ignoring it is unrealistic.

Give a little, take it back rule
PatternExample
While / Although + clause, main clauseWhile both sides make valid points, the evidence is mixed.
Admittedly, … ; nevertheless, …Admittedly, rumours are old; nevertheless, …
Granted (that) + clause, main clauseGranted that not every post is accurate, …
It is true that … However, …It is true that apps connect people. However, …
Despite / In spite of + noun or -ingDespite its risks, … · Despite being popular, …

Three rules

  • One connector only: Although it is useful, but it is risky. ✗ → Although it is useful, it is risky. ✓
  • Despite + noun / -ing: Despite it is popular ✗ → Despite its popularity ✓ · despite of ✗
  • Give first, take back second: the second half of the sentence carries the writer’s real view.
Fix it correct
Broken sentenceFixed sentence
1. Although it is useful, but it can be harmful.
2. Despite of the risks, millions of people use it daily.
3. Despite it is popular, the app has many critics.
4. Admittedly that some posts are false, most are not.
5. While apps connect people. They also divide them.
6. In spite of it has risks, the app is still popular.
7. Although it is risky, however it is useful.
8. Granted that rules are needed, but they must be fair.

The scholar’s tool: the debate courtyard

10 MIN

Dunhuang was one of the Silk Road’s great meeting points: texts in many languages and from many traditions were later found side by side in a single cave library. A discursive text is a meeting place like that. Two sides sit opposite each other in the courtyard; the judge listens to both before speaking.

The two wings are the same size: a fair text gives each side similar space. Side 1 is the side the text presents first, Side 2 the other one. The steps are the concessions, and the seat at the top is the verdict.

Part of the courtyardReading moveQuestion you ask
The gateFind the issueWhat question does the text discuss? (introduction)
Side 1 / Side 2Collect the argumentsWhat does each side claim — and with what evidence?
The stepsNotice concessionsWhere does the writer admit a point to the other side? (admittedly, granted that, while)
The poolFind common groundWhat would both sides accept?
The judge’s seatFind the verdictWhat does the writer decide in the end — and why?
Compare it think

Youwrite one sidewrite both sidesfollow one argumentread and judge two sides
The viewfrom the first linein the conclusionnorth: the positionthe judge’s verdict, near the end

Sit in the judge’s chair

CONTINUED

Two short sources (written for this book) answer the same question: Should social media users have to post under their real names?

Source A · A newspaper column
Online abuse thrives on anonymity. People write things behind a fake name that they would never say face to face. If every account showed a real name, most users would think twice before posting insults or spreading misinformation, and victims would know who had attacked them.
Source B · A journalist’s blog
Anonymity protects people as well as hurting them. A student who reports cheating, or a young person who asks for help with a family problem, may only speak because nobody knows who they are. Besides, serious abusers can already be traced by the police without a public real-name rule.

Zarina (a fictional student) read both sources with her courtyard map and wrote this comparative response.

The gate
(1) Sources A and B disagree about whether online anonymity does more harm than good.
Side 1
(2) Source A argues that a real-name rule would make users behave more responsibly and would reduce abuse and misinformation.
Side 2
(3) Source B, in contrast, claims that anonymity protects vulnerable people, such as students who report cheating. (4) It also points out that the police can already trace serious abusers.
The judge
(5) Admittedly, Source A identifies a real problem: insults are easier behind a fake name. (6) Nevertheless, Source B appears to be more convincing, because it shows that a real-name rule would silence the people who most need protection. (7) On balance, better reporting tools seem fairer than forcing every user to reveal their identity.

LEVEL 2

Hear both sides

Should Influencers Label Every Paid Post? · A short discursive text · written for this book · about 160 words
Online influencers now sell products to millions of young followers, and many countries are debating whether every paid post should carry a clear label. Influencers often argue that compulsory labels are unnecessary. In their view, followers trust them because they are honest, and a large “AD” sign makes personal content look like television advertising. They also point out that most viewers already know when a product has been sent as a gift. Consumer groups, by contrast, maintain that young viewers often cannot tell a personal opinion from a paid promotion. When money changes hands, they argue, the audience has a right to know. Granted that labels may make some posts look less personal, this cost seems small compared with the risk of misleading teenagers. On balance, a short, clear label appears to be the fairer solution: it protects the most vulnerable followers and, in the long run, may even strengthen the trust that honest creators depend on.

CriterionA C1 fair report of a debate …

V · Vocabularyuses precise topic words and collocations in an academic tone
G · Grammaruses a range of structures with few errors; in this stop: concession structures (While / Although + clause · Admittedly, … ; nevertheless, … · Granted that … · despite + noun / -ing)

While some critics may be cautious about new technology, many of their concerns rest on evidence. · Admittedly, some young people spend a lot of time online; nevertheless, many still value face-to-face talk. · Granted that some rules could limit free speech, sensible regulation may also protect users. · It is true that popular posts reach many people. 3

Read like a detective

17 MIN

Before you read: skim only the title and the six section headings. What will the writer’s answer be?  AI is good   AI is bad   “yes, but …”

The Patient Tutor: What AI Can — and Cannot — Do for Learning

A long-read feature · about 960 words · B2–C1 · written for this book (Dilshod is fictional) · continues on the next page
The writer changes direction four times. Can you find all four turns?

AIt is almost midnight in a student hostel in Navoi. Dilshod has a statistics test in the morning, and the formula for standard deviation still makes no sense to him. His teacher is asleep, his friends are as confused as he is, and the textbook explains the idea in exactly the same way it did three hours ago. So he opens a chatbot and types: “Explain this to me as if I were twelve.” Within seconds, he has a simple explanation, an example about football scores and an offer to test him with three practice questions.

BScenes like this one are now repeated in hostels and kitchens all over the world, and they have divided educators. Some see artificial intelligence (AI) as the most powerful learning tool since the printed book; others see it as a machine for avoiding thought. This article argues that both groups are partly right. AI can become a remarkably patient tutor, but only if universities change what they ask students to do. The real danger is not that students will cheat. It is that they will outsource the very thinking that learning requires.

1 · A tutor for everyone?

CThe case for AI begins with an old idea. Educational researchers have long observed that students who receive one-to-one tutoring tend to learn more than students taught in large groups. A good tutor notices exactly where a learner is confused, gives a personalised explanation and adjusts the next question to the learner’s level. The difficulty has always been cost: no country can afford a personal tutor for every student.

DThis is precisely where AI tools appear to offer something new. Such a tool never loses patience, never makes a learner feel foolish for asking the same question twice and gives instant feedback at midnight before an exam. For students who are too shy to ask questions in class, or who study in a second or third language, these qualities may matter even more than the accuracy of any single answer. Supporters therefore argue that AI could make a privilege of the few available to the many.

2 · Answers without understanding

EHowever, the same features that make AI attractive also make it risky. A tutor and an answer machine can look very similar on a screen, but they do very different jobs. The former asks questions, waits and lets the student struggle a little; the latter simply delivers a finished product. Learning scientists often describe this struggle as “productive”: when we work hard to retrieve an idea or solve a problem, we tend to remember it longer. If a chatbot removes the struggle, it may also remove the learning.

FThis problem is most serious in writing. An essay is not only a product to be handed in; it is a way of discovering what one thinks. A student who asks a machine to “write 500 words on climate change” receives a text, but skips the slow work of choosing an argument, finding evidence and connecting ideas. Such a student may submit a fluent assignment and still be unable to explain its main point. In other words, the grade improves while the skill does not.

Öqiş va yozuv amaliyotiModule 3 · Practical class 22
3

Read like a detective

CONTINUED
The Patient Tutor · continued

3 · “It is only a tool”

GDefenders of AI reply that every new technology has caused similar fears. When pocket calculators entered classrooms, many teachers worried that students would forget how to do arithmetic. Today, few people would ban calculators from a physics exam. Admittedly, this comparison has some force: tools do change which skills matter, and education must adapt to them.

HYet the comparison breaks down at an important point. A calculator performs one narrow operation that the student has already learned to understand; it does not decide what the problem is or how to approach it. A chatbot, by contrast, can perform almost the entire task, from planning to final wording. The question, therefore, is not whether students should use tools, but which parts of the thinking they should keep for themselves.

4 · Who gets the patient tutor?

IThere is also a question of fairness. The best AI tools often require a fast internet connection, a modern device and, increasingly, a paid subscription. In addition, many tools still work better in English than in Uzbek, Karakalpak or Tajik. These gaps mean that the students who could gain most from a free tutor — those in rural areas or with weaker English — may be the last to receive a good one. If universities ignore this, AI could widen the very inequality that its supporters hope to reduce.

5 · Redesigning the task

JNone of these concerns, however, leads to the conclusion that AI should be banned. Bans are difficult to enforce, and they leave students unprepared for workplaces where such tools are already common. A more promising response is to redesign assessment so that the thinking stays visible. Teachers can ask students to submit a plan and a first draft alongside the final text, to explain their argument in a short oral discussion, or to add a brief note describing how they used AI and what they changed.

KSome universities are also experimenting with assignments that use AI openly: students ask a chatbot for an answer and then evaluate it, find its errors and improve it. Tasks of this kind turn the machine from a ghost writer into a sparring partner. They also teach a skill that will matter long after graduation: judging whether a confident-sounding answer is actually correct.

Holding on to the thread

LDilshod’s midnight explanation may well help him pass his test. Whether it helps him learn statistics depends on what happens next: does he try the three practice questions, or does he ask the machine to answer them too? The same choice faces universities. Used carelessly, AI offers answers without understanding. Used wisely, within tasks that keep students thinking, it could offer something education has rarely been able to afford — a patient tutor for everyone.

Jigsaw option · the caravan. Five groups, five camels: A–B + L (the leader: thesis and conclusion) · C–D · E–F · G–H · I–K. Each group writes its step on one card. Then the five groups stand in a line and read their cards in order. Check that each card follows from the one before.

Language toolkit: reference words

10 MIN

Reference words (the knots in the rope) point back to something the writer has already said, so that it does not have to be repeated.

Notice find it

Find these sentences in the article and complete them.

1. (D) is precisely where AI tools appear to offer something new.

2. (D) tool never loses patience …

3. (E) The asks questions …; the simply delivers a finished product.

6. (K) Tasks of kind turn the machine from a ghost writer into a sparring partner.

Four knots rule
Knot + patternPoints back to …Example from the article
this + singular nounone idea just mentionedThis problem is most serious …
these + plural nounseveral things just mentionedThese gaps mean that …
such a + sing. · such + pl.a thing of that kindSuch a student may submit …
the former / the latterthe 1st / 2nd of exactly twoThe former asks; the latter delivers.

Three rules

  • Add a noun. A lonely This can point to three things; This problem points to one.
  • Word order: such a tool ✓  ·  a such tool ✗  ·  such tools ✓  ·  such a tools ✗
  • Two only: the former / the latter = two things. For three or more, say the first … the last.

The scholar’s tool: the caravan rope

On the Silk Road, the camels of a caravan were tied together in one long line, and the caravan leader held the front of the rope. A long article is built the same way: the thesis leads, every section is a camel, and the reference words are the knots that tie each camel to the one before.

A short text can be followed from memory. For a long text, write one short note per section.

In the caravanIn a long articleWhat you do as a reader

A camel that pulls backan objection (often after however, yet, admittedly)Mark it O. Then find the writer’s reply.
The bell on the last camelthe conclusionCompare it with the thesis: same claim, new words?

How to make an argument map in four moves

  • Find the leader. Read the introduction and the conclusion first. Underline the thesis.
  • One box per camel. Use the headings. Write what each step adds — max. 10 words, your own words.
  • Write the knots between the boxes: This …, Such …, However, Yet, Admittedly …
  • Ring the bell. Compare the last box with the first: both should state the same claim.

LEVEL 2

Map a new rope

Letter to the editor · a reply to “The Patient Tutor” · written for this book

① Your article made a strong case for redesigning tasks. I would go further: universities should teach students how to use AI from their very first semester. Silence on this subject does not stop students from using such tools; it only means that they use them badly. ② There are two reasons for this view. The first is practical: graduates will enter workplaces where AI is part of daily work. The second is educational: when students learn to question a chatbot’s answer, they practise exactly the critical reading that university should develop. Of these two reasons, the latter seems to me the more important. ③ Admittedly, some students will misuse AI however carefully they are trained. This risk is real. Yet it is far greater when nobody shows them what good use looks like. ④ In short, the question is no longer whether our students will use AI, but whether they will use it well.

Read like a detective

17 MIN

Before you read: count the names in brackets on this page and the next. How many different scholars speak in this article?  

Two Tongues, One Mind? Revisiting the “Bilingual Advantage”

Malika Rashidova & Daniel Wren · 2024 · Caravan Journal of Language and Mind, 7(2), 45–63 · about 510 words · a fictional journal and article, written for this book
Underline each reporting verb and the scholar it belongs to.

1 · Introduction

AIn Uzbekistan, as in much of the world, growing up with more than one language is ordinary rather than exceptional. A child in Tashkent may speak Uzbek at home, hear Russian in the street and study English at school. For much of the twentieth century, however, parents were often warned that two languages might confuse young children and slow down their progress at school. More recently, the opposite message has become popular: that bilingualism gives the brain a daily “workout” and produces sharper thinkers. This article reviews the research behind both claims and argues that neither tells the whole story.

2 · Review of the literature

2.1 From “confusion” to “advantage”

BEarly studies of bilingual children frequently reported lower scores on vocabulary and intelligence tests (see Haydarov, 2009, for a review). Haydarov (2009) points out, however, that many of these studies compared bilingual children from poorer families with monolingual children from wealthier ones, and often tested them only in their weaker language. When such differences were taken into account, the so-called bilingual disadvantage largely disappeared.

CA more optimistic picture emerged in the following decades. Several studies have suggested that bilinguals perform better on tasks that require attention and switching between rules (Lindqvist & Berg, 2012; Tursunova, 2014). Lindqvist and Berg (2012) argue that bilinguals constantly practise controlling two active languages and that this practice strengthens general mental control. Mirzayev (2015) goes further, claiming that lifelong bilingualism may protect the ageing brain. Such claims attracted wide attention from journalists and parents, and the “bilingual advantage” soon became common knowledge.

2.2 The replication problem

DHowever, the advantage has proved difficult to replicate. In a large study of adults, Okafor et al. (2018) found no consistent difference between bilinguals and monolinguals on any of their attention tasks. Brennan (2019) observes that studies with positive results are more likely to be published than studies that find nothing, which may have made the advantage look larger than it really is. On this basis, some researchers reject the idea of a general advantage altogether (Okafor et al., 2018), while others maintain that it exists but appears only under certain conditions (Tursunova, 2014; Yusupova, 2021).

While you read · Who says what? match

a found no clear difference in adults · b early studies compared unequal groups · c using two languages trains mental control · d positive results are published more often · e bilingualism may protect the ageing brain

Öqiş va yozuv amaliyotiModule 3 · Practical class 23
3

Read like a detective

CONTINUED
Two Tongues, One Mind? · continued

2.3 From “whether” to “which kind”

ERather than asking whether bilingualism makes people cleverer, recent work examines which kinds of bilingual experience matter. Yusupova (2021) compared university students in Samarkand who switched between Uzbek and Russian many times a day with students who used their second language mainly in class. The first group performed better on attention tasks, and Yusupova concludes that “how often and how flexibly two languages are used may matter more than the label ‘bilingual’ itself” (p. 112). This view echoes an earlier image by Ahmedova (2016, as cited in Yusupova, 2021), who described bilingualism as “a dial, not a switch”.

2.4 The gap

FTaken together, the literature supports neither of the simple stories that parents are told. Two languages do not confuse children, but they do not automatically create better thinkers either. What remains unclear is how everyday patterns of language use in multilingual societies such as Uzbekistan shape attention and learning. The present study addresses this gap by following schoolchildren in three regions of Uzbekistan over two school years.

[Sections 3–6 of the article — Method, Results, Discussion and Conclusion — are not printed here.]

References

Brennan, T. (2019). Why good news travels faster: Publication bias in bilingualism research. Oasis Studies in Psychology, 25(2), 140–158. https://doi.org/10.0000/osp.2019.2502

Haydarov, S. (2009). Two languages at the school gate: Bilingual children in Central Asian classrooms. Minaret Press.

Lindqvist, M., & Berg, A. (2012). Switching rules, switching languages: Mental control in young bilinguals. Registan Review of Applied Linguistics, 3(1), 12–29. https://doi.org/10.0000/rral.2012.0301

Mirzayev, J. (2015). The bilingual brain across the lifespan: A review. Oasis Studies in Psychology, 21(4), 377–395. https://doi.org/10.0000/osp.2015.2104

Okafor, L., Petrova, K., & Salimov, R. (2018). Looking for the bilingual advantage in adults: A large-scale test. Caravan Journal of Language and Mind, 1(2), 88–107. https://doi.org/10.0000/cjlm.2018.0102

Tursunova, G. (2014). Daily language use and attention in Uzbek–Russian bilingual teenagers. In K. Saidov (Ed.), Language and thought in Central Asia (pp. 55–74). Silk Road Academic Press.

The italics rule: italicise the thing on the shelf — the book title, the journal name and the volume number. Article and chapter titles stay plain. Capitals: article and book titles in sentence case (first word + after a colon + names); journal names in Title Case.

Spot the mistakes detect

A student copied three cards from the article. Compare them with the article’s list: there are seven mistakes. Find at least four and correct them below.

1. Yusupova, Nodira (2021). How Often, Not How Many: Language Switching And Attention In University Students. Registan Review of Applied Linguistics, 12(2), 101–118. https://doi.org/10.0000/rral.2021.1202

2. Okafor, L. et al. (2018). Looking for the bilingual advantage in adults: A large-scale test. Caravan Journal of Language and Mind, 1(2), 88–107. https://doi.org/10.0000/cjlm.2018.0102

3. Brennan, T. (2019). Why good news travels faster: Publication bias in bilingualism research. Oasis Studies in Psychology, 140–158.

Model: a mini literature review · B2+ · written for this book

Does growing up with two languages help children? Early studies reported lower scores for bilingual children (Haydarov, 2009). Later, several studies suggested that bilinguals are better at attention tasks (Lindqvist & Berg, 2012; Tursunova, 2014). However, Okafor et al. (2018) found no difference in adults. Yusupova (2021) argues that how often people switch languages is more important.

☆This model is B2+. Upgrade two of its sentences with the Level-up tools.

Read a new passage

From a literature review · written for this book · all sources are fictional

(1) For many years, switching between languages in class was seen as a sign of weak language skills. (2) Karimov and Lee (2020), however, argue that limited code-switching can help students to understand difficult content. (3) Similar benefits have been reported for younger children (Field, 2023; Rahimova, 2019). (4) In migrant families, the picture is less positive: Novak et al. (2022) found that children who rarely heard their heritage language at home gradually lost it. (5) Abdullayeva (2017) describes a Samarkand family in which three languages “share the dinner table without fighting” (p. 41). (6) An earlier study is far more ambitious: Usmonova (2014, as cited in Rahimova, 2019) claims that every bilingual school produces stronger readers. (7) Clearly, therefore, every lesson in every school should be taught in two languages.

Be the examiner

7 MIN

Examiners use four criteria. Use them to mark two students’ work, then apply them to your own citation report.

CriterionA C1 citation report …
T · Taskanswers the exact question and keeps the writers’ own voice apart from the voices they cite
O · Organisationhas one point per sentence (source → what it says → how the writers use it) and links ideas with more than Firstly / Secondly
V · Vocabularyuses precise topic words and collocations in an academic tone
G · Grammaruses a range of structures with few errors; in this stop: reporting verbs and citation patterns (Okafor et al. (2018) found …; (Lindqvist & Berg, 2012); as cited in)

Score each criterion: 1 = not yet · 2 = almost · 3 = yes

Two students answered the question Who speaks in paragraph D, and how far do the writers trust each source? in about 70 words. Mark both.

Student A
In paragraph D the writers talk about the replication problem. Okafor et al. (2018) proved that bilinguals and monolinguals are the same, so the advantage is fake. Brennan (2019) says that positive studies are published more, this is very interesting. Some researchers reject the idea (Okafor et al., 2018), but others think it exists only sometimes (Tursunova, 2014; Yusupova, 2021).
Student B
Paragraph D sets out the case against a general advantage. The writers first report a large study in which Okafor et al. (2018) found no consistent difference between bilingual and monolingual adults; the verb found shows that they accept this result. They then cite Brennan (2019), who observes that positive results are more likely to be published. Finally, they contrast researchers who reject the advantage with those who maintain that it appears only under certain conditions.

Which criterion shows the biggest difference between A and B? Why?

☆Be the editor: rewrite two sentences of Student A so they meet the C1 column.

Word Bazaar

Twelve words for reading research on motivation: six about the mind, six about the study itself.

intrinsicADJ coming from inside a person: interest, curiosity, enjoymentintrinsic motivation
extrinsicADJ coming from outside a person: grades, prizes, praiseextrinsic rewards
incentiveNOUN something offered to encourage a person to actoffer an incentive
autonomyNOUN the freedom to make your own decisionsa sense of autonomy
persistenceNOUN continuing with a task even when it is difficultpersistence in a long course
procrastinationNOUN delaying a task you know you should do nowreduce procrastination
self-efficacyNOUN belief in your own ability to succeed at a tasklow self-efficacy in writing
engagementNOUN how actively and attentively you take partstudent engagement
participantsNOUN the people who take part in a study124 participants
findingsNOUN the results that a study reportsThe findings suggest …
implicationNOUN what a result means for future practice or researchimplications for teachers
significantADJ (in statistics) unlikely to be the result of chancea significant difference

Read like a detective

17 MIN

Four abstracts · about 450 words in all. Before you read: using the titles only, which study suits an essay on “Why do students give up?”  

Find the five scenes in each abstract.

ABSTRACT 1 · Oasis Studies in Psychology, 31(2) · about 180 words · a fictional study, written for this book

Choice and the Reluctant Reader: Text Choice and Reading Motivation in University EFL Classes

Dilfuza Normatova & James Carver

A1(1)Many university students in English as a foreign language (EFL) programmes read only what is required. (2)Research on motivation suggests that a sense of autonomy can increase intrinsic motivation, but few studies have tested this idea in Central Asian classrooms. (3)This study examines whether giving students a choice of reading texts affects their reading motivation and persistence. (4)Over one semester, 124 second-year students at two Uzbek universities were divided into two groups. (5)One group chose their weekly texts from a list of six; the other read texts selected by the teacher. (6)Motivation was measured with a questionnaire at the start and end of the semester, and persistence was recorded as the number of optional texts each student finished. (7)Students in the choice group reported significantly higher intrinsic motivation at the end of the semester and completed almost twice as many optional texts. (8)However, no difference was found in test scores. (9)These findings suggest that small changes in task design may increase motivation at no extra cost. (10)Teachers are encouraged to offer a limited choice of texts rather than complete freedom.

Keywords: autonomy, intrinsic motivation, EFL reading, choice

ABSTRACT 2 · Minaret Studies in Education, 12(4) · about 110 words · a fictional study, written for this book

“I Will Start Tomorrow”: How First-Year Students Explain Their Procrastination

Sardor Qodirov

A2(1)Procrastination is often described as a problem of poor time management. (2)Recent research, however, has increasingly treated it as a problem of emotion rather than planning. (3)The aim of this study was to explore how first-year students explain their own procrastination. (4)Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 18 students from three faculties of a university in Samarkand, and the transcripts were analysed thematically. (5)Three main themes emerged: fear of producing imperfect work, unclear task instructions and low confidence in one’s own ability. (6)Surprisingly, students rarely mentioned a lack of time. (7)The results indicate that procrastination is closely linked to self-efficacy. (8)Universities may reduce procrastination by giving clearer instructions and early, low-stakes feedback.

Keywords: procrastination, self-efficacy, first-year students, interviews

While you read · Scenes in Abstract 1 label

Write B background · A aim · M method · R results · C conclusion for each sentence.

ABSTRACT 3 · Oasis Studies in Psychology, 29(1) · about 105 words · a fictional review, written for this book

Do Rewards Kill Interest? A Review of Classroom Research on Extrinsic Incentives

Laylo Hamidova, Peter Strand & Aziza Murodova

A3(1)Teachers often use rewards such as points, stickers or prizes to encourage effort. (2)Whether such incentives support or undermine intrinsic motivation, however, remains a matter of debate. (3)This article reviews classroom studies of the effects of extrinsic rewards on students’ interest and engagement. (4)The review shows that rewards tend to reduce intrinsic motivation when they are expected and given simply for doing a task. (5)In contrast, unexpected rewards, and rewards that give information about progress, do not appear to have this effect. (6)It is argued that the type of reward matters more than its presence. (7)Implications for the design of gamified learning apps are discussed.

Keywords: extrinsic rewards, intrinsic motivation, review, gamification

Motivation and Mobile Apps
