Language toolkit: present or past?

10 MIN

An abstract changes tense as it moves from scene to scene. The rule is simple: what is still true now → present; what the researchers did and found → past.

Notice find it

Find the verbs in the abstracts and complete the sentences.

1. (A1·2) Research that …

2. (A1·2) few studies this idea

3. (A1·3) This study whether …

4. (A1·4) 124 students into …

5. (A1·7) The choice group …

6. (A1·9) These findings that …

7. (A2·3) The aim to explore …

8. (A3·4) The review that …

The tense map rule
SceneUsual tense · whyExample
Backgroundpresent / pres. perfect · true nowResearch suggests … · few studies have tested …
Aimpast simple (or present)This study examined whether … · This study examines …
Methodpast, often passive · finishedStudents were divided … · data were collected
Resultspast · (a review: often present)Students reported … · The review shows …
Conclusionpresent + may · what it means nowThese findings suggest that … may …
  • No future in an abstract. The study is finished: In this paper we will discuss ✗ → This paper discusses ✓
  • Aim: both tenses appear in real abstracts; in your own abstract (Stop 44) use the past simple.
  • Found = past, means = present. Students read more (past). This suggests that choice matters (present).
  • Passive for the method: the people doing the work are not important — Data were collected …
Fix it correct
Broken sentenceFixed sentence
1. In this paper we will examine students’ motivation.
2. In 2024, eighteen students are interviewed.
3. The results shows that rewards reduce interest.
4. Participants were completed a questionnaire.
5. These findings suggested that teachers today should …

verb → noun		measure → measurement · conclude → conclusion · persist → persistenceMotivation was measured twice. → The measurement of motivation at two points is a strength.

A Persian miniature shows a whole story in one small painting: the sky, the travellers, the work, the harvest and the road out of the picture. An abstract is the miniature of a research article: five scenes, inside the frame of the title, painted with a few keywords.

Read the abstract first; then decide whether you need the full article.

5

Look closer: a model analysis

CONTINUED

Below, Abstract 1 is divided into its scenes. It is followed by a short abstract analysis: a reader’s evaluation that ends with a verdict.

Background · 1–2
A classroom problem (students read only what is required) → what research suggests → the gap: few studies have tested this in Central Asia. PRESENT
Aim · 3
This study examines whether text choice affects motivation and persistence. PRESENT
Method · 4–6
124 students, two universities, one semester, two groups; motivation was measured by questionnaire, persistence was recorded as optional texts finished. PAST PASSIVE
Results · 7–8
Choice group reported higher motivation and read more; however, no difference was found in test scores. PAST
Conclusion · 9–10
These findings suggest that task design may increase motivation; teachers are encouraged to offer limited choice. PRESENT + MAY

Model analysis · about 120 words · written for this book

[1] Abstract 1, a fictional study in Oasis Studies in Psychology, follows the classic five-scene structure. [2] It opens with two sentences of background, moving from a common classroom problem to a gap in the research. [3] The aim is stated clearly in the present tense. [4] The method takes three sentences in the past passive and gives the key details: who, how many, how long and how motivation was measured. [5] The results, in the past tense, include a negative finding about test scores, which makes the abstract more trustworthy. [6] The conclusion returns to the present and is suitably cautious (may). [7] Overall, the abstract is complete and balanced; it does not explain, however, how the six texts were chosen.

1. Which sentence [1–7] gives the analyst’s own judgement? Which two describe tense?

2. Why does a “no difference” result make an abstract more trustworthy?

☆3. The analysis is in the present tense, but the study is in the past. Why?

4. Before citing Abstract 1 in an essay, what else would you want to know?

☆5. This model is B2+. Upgrade two of its sentences with the Level-up tools.

The two-minute routine

10 s · frame: title + keywords20 s · the aim sentence20 s · who? how many? how?40 s · the main result30 s · does the conclusion go further than the results?

Then decide: read in full   keep for later   skip. Try it with Abstract 3.

Two new abstracts

Your question: How can online English courses keep adult learners from giving up?

ABSTRACT 5 · Minaret Studies in Education, 13(1) · a fictional study, written for this book

A Friend on the Course: Peer Messages and Persistence in Online English Learning

(1) Online language courses often lose many learners in the first weeks. (2) This study investigated whether short weekly messages from a peer “study buddy” help learners to persist. (3) 210 adult learners on a free online English course were randomly assigned to a buddy group or a control group. (4) After eight weeks, 61% of the buddy group were still active, compared with 38% of the control group. (5) Peer encouragement is therefore the best way to keep online learners motivated.

ABSTRACT 6 · Oasis Studies in Psychology, 30(2) · a fictional study, written for this book

Badges in the Classroom: Digital Rewards and Engagement in Primary-School English Lessons

(1) Digital badges are now common in children’s learning apps. (2) This study examined whether badges for completed tasks affect pupils’ engagement in English lessons. (3) Forty-six pupils aged 9–10 at one school in Bukhara used a classroom app with or without badges for six weeks, and their teachers recorded how many tasks each pupil completed. (4) The badge group completed more tasks in the first two weeks, but by week six the difference had disappeared. (5) Badges may therefore raise engagement only for a short time.

Examiners use four criteria. Use them to mark two students’ work, then apply them to your own source decision.

CriterionA C1 source decision …

Score each criterion: 1 = not yet · 2 = almost · 3 = yes

A classmate is writing an essay on “Do rewards help or harm students’ motivation?” Should she read the full article behind Abstract 3? Two students answered in about 70 words. Mark both.

Student A
Abstract 3 is a review about rewards and motivation. The review shows that expected rewards reduce interest, but unexpected rewards does not have this effect. It is a very interesting topic, and rewards are used in every school. In my opinion rewards are bad, because my little brother only studies for stickers. So she must read it.
Student B
Abstract 3 reports a review of classroom studies, so it speaks directly to her question. It shows that expected rewards tend to reduce intrinsic motivation, whereas unexpected or informative rewards do not appear to have this effect. The results are carefully hedged; a notable limitation, however, is that the abstract does not say how many studies were reviewed. She should therefore read the full article, starting with its method.

Word Bazaar

Twelve words for discussing history and the way it is written. Test a partner: read the meaning, they say the word.

accountNOUN a spoken or written description of eventsa detailed account of the battle

emotiveADJ chosen to cause strong feelings in the readeremotive words such as “heroic”

Read like a detective

17 MIN

History and memory. For many people, a school textbook is the only history book they ever read carefully, so its voice matters. Below are two extracts about the same event — how papermaking reached Samarkand — written for this book in the style of real textbooks (two extracts · about 580 words in all). Are the facts the same? Is the voice?

Before you read: which will be more objective?   a school book for children   a university textbook   no difference

Extract A · The Gift of Samarkand

From a fictional school history book · written for this book · about 250 words

AEveryone knows that the finest paper of the medieval world was made in Samarkand. The story began in 751, at the great Battle of Talas, when the brave armies of the Islamic world defeated the mighty forces of China. Among the prisoners taken in that battle were skilled craftsmen who knew how to make paper. For centuries, the Chinese had jealously hidden this secret from the rest of humanity. Now the secret was finally free.

BThe craftsmen were brought to Samarkand, and there they shared their knowledge. However, these men soon discovered that the masters of our city were not simple pupils. Our ancestors did not just copy the foreign method; they perfected it. Using cotton and linen instead of tree bark, they produced sheets that were smoother, stronger and whiter than any others. In a few short years, Samarkand paper was famous from Baghdad to Cairo, and no ruler wanted to write on anything else.

CThis wonderful invention changed the world. Thanks to Samarkand, the libraries of the Islamic world were filled with books, and great scholars were able to write and copy their works. Without the genius of our ancestors, these scholars would never have produced their famous books, and Europe would have remained in darkness for many more centuries.

DToday, the paper workshops near Samarkand remind every visitor of this glorious past. It is clear that paper was the greatest gift that Central Asia ever gave to the world, and every young citizen should be proud of it.

Count the words that carry feelings. Then count the sources.

Glossary

craft — a skill of making things by hand · parchment — animal skin prepared for writing on · rags — old pieces of cloth · patron — a rich person who pays for art or learning · the Abbasids, the Tang — ruling dynasties of the time

While you read

Underline every fact you could check (a date, a place, a name). Circle every word that tells you what to feel. Which wins in A? In B?

Judge Extract A by its evidence, not by its tone: it gives no source for any of its claims.
Öqiş va yozuv amaliyotiModule 3 · Practical class 25
3

The second voice

CONTINUED

Extract B · Paper on the Silk Road

From a fictional university textbook · written for this book · about 320 words

APaper was first developed in China, probably around two thousand years ago, and for several centuries it was used mainly in East Asia. How the craft reached the Islamic world, however, is less certain than many popular accounts suggest.

BA well-known story links the arrival of papermaking in Samarkand to the Battle of Talas in 751, where Abbasid forces and their allies defeated an army of the Tang dynasty. According to this story, which appears in later Arabic writings, Chinese prisoners taught the craft to local workers. Some historians accept the account; many do not. The sources that report it were written long after the battle, and the earliest ones give few details. Moreover, some evidence suggests that paper was already known in parts of Central Asia before 751, probably through trade with China. If so, the prisoners may have improved an existing craft rather than introduced a new one.

CWhat is better documented is the result. Within a few decades, Samarkand had become an important centre of paper production, and the craft spread westwards, reaching Baghdad by around the end of the eighth century. Local paper makers appear to have used rags and other plant fibres, which were easier to find than the materials used in China. The new writing material was cheaper than parchment, and historians generally link its spread to a sharp increase in the number of books and official documents produced in cities such as Baghdad.

DThe importance of this change should not be overstated, nor should it be ignored. Paper did not create scholarship on its own; libraries, teachers and patrons also played their part. Still, it made knowledge easier to copy, to store and to share.

EThe story of Samarkand paper therefore shows both the value and the limits of historical memory. The city’s role in spreading the craft is widely accepted; the details of how it began are not. A careful reader should keep the two apart.

Same event. Find one fact that BOTH extracts share.
Jigsaw option. Group A becomes the expert on Extract A, Group B on Extract B (paragraphs A–C), Group C on Extract B (paragraphs D–E). Each group lists (1) the facts and (2) the feelings in its part. Then form mixed groups of three and compare your lists.
Talk after reading: Which extract would you put in a school textbook? What would you change in it first? Why?

4Paper was the greatest gift that Central Asia ever gave to the world. (A, para D)

Language toolkit: cohesion devices

10 MIN

Good writers do not repeat the same noun in every sentence. They tie sentences together with small words and chains of related words. This is cohesion. A careful reader follows the ties.

Notice find it

Find the missing word in Extract B. What does it replace?

Extract BMissing wordIt replaces …
1. (B) Some historians accept the account; many ___ not.
2. (B) … and the earliest ___ give few details.
3. (B) If ___, the prisoners may have improved …
4. (B) … rather than introduced a new ___.
5. (E) … the details of how it began are not Ø.—Ø =
The ties that hold a text rule
DeviceHow it worksExample from the extracts
Reference (Stop 22)this, these, it point backPaper was first developed in China … it was used mainly in East Asia.
Substitutionone(s) → noun · do / did → verb phrase · so / not → clausethe earliest ones · many do not · If so, …
Ellipsisrepeated words are left out (Ø)… how it began are not Ø.
Lexical chainsynonyms, general words, word familiespaper → the craft → papermaking → the new writing material

Three rules

  • one replaces countable nouns only: a new one (= book) ✓ · a new one (= information) ✗
  • Keep the auxiliary in ellipsis: Some agree, but most do not ✓ · most not ✗
  • Every this / such / one must have a clear partner earlier in the text. No partner = no cohesion.
Fix it tie it

Rewrite the second part with substitution or ellipsis so that nothing is repeated.

1. The old book praised the ruler; the new book did not praise the ruler. →

2. Some sources are reliable, but many sources are not reliable. →

3. Was the story invented? Some historians think that it was invented. →

At C1 an objectivity analysis must itself be objective. You judge the text in degrees, not in black and white; you admit what it does well; and you name exactly what it leaves out.

ToolPhrasesExample
Degree words
judge in degrees		largely · partly · broadly · far less … thanExtract A is largely celebratory and only partly factual.
Concession
admit, then judge		While …, … · Although the extract is useful for …, it …While Extract A gets the date right, it never says how it knows.
Nominalisation
verb / adjective → noun		omit → omission · absent → absence · use → the use ofThe omission of the historians’ debate weakens Extract A.
Precise text verbs
what the text does		presents · implies · overstates · acknowledgesExtract B acknowledges the doubt; Extract A overstates the role of paper.

The scholar’s tool: the mirror

10 MIN

In the old bazaars of Tabriz, a mirror-maker held a sheet of glass up to the light before he sold it. A good mirror shows the world as it is. A bad one bends it. When you read a history text, hold up the scholar’s mirror: five parts, five questions.

An objective text lets the reader separate the facts (the glass) from the writer’s framing.

Mirror part · checkAsk yourselfSignals in the text
The glass · factsCould I check this in another source?dates, places, names, events
The frame · loaded wordsWhich words tell me what to feel?brave, glorious, jealously, genius
The angle · balanceWhat is in — and what is left out?some historians … many do not
The lamp · sourcesWho says so? How do they know?according to …; later writings report
The mist · certaintyToo sure — or carefully unsure?it is clear ↔ probably, appear to
Compare it think

QuestionHow sure is the writer?What are the two sides?Is the whole text fair?
You look athedging wordsarguments, concessionsall five mirror parts
You producea hedged comparisona comparative answeran objectivity analysis

5

Hold up the mirror: a model analysis

CONTINUED

Extract C · The Greatest Road · from a fictional guidebook for schools, written for this book

The Silk Road was without doubt the greatest highway in human history. For more than a thousand years, brave merchants travelled the whole way from China to Rome with camels loaded with precious silk. Our cities were the jewels of this road, and all the knowledge of the world passed through them. Every historian agrees that without Central Asia there would have been no trade between East and West.

The model: a student held Extract C up to the mirror and wrote this analysis (130 words).

Verdict first
(1) Extract C is only partly objective.
The glass
(2) Its factual core — that silk travelled west from China through Central Asian cities — can be checked in other sources.
The frame
(3) However, the writer surrounds these facts with emotive language such as “brave”, “precious” and “jewels”, which tells the reader what to feel.
The angle
(4) The picture is also narrow: the extract suggests that merchants travelled the whole route, whereas most historians believe that goods usually passed through many hands.
The lamp + mist
(5) Moreover, no source is given, and phrases such as “without doubt” and “every historian agrees” claim far more certainty than the evidence allows.
Conclusion
(6) Overall, the extract is useful for its basic facts, but it should be read as a celebration of the past rather than as a neutral account of it.

1. Which sentence gives the overall judgement? Why does it come first?

☆2. Find the lexical chain for “Extract C” in the analysis (e.g. the writer …).

3. Which linking words move the analysis from part to part?

☆4. Sentence (4) uses whereas. What two things does it compare?

5. In sentence (6), what does it in “a neutral account of it” refer to?

the past   the extract   the evidence

6. Does the student say Extract C is useless? Underline the words that show balance.

Tool tips: According to … · Historians generally agree that … · one of the … · appears to · some … while others …

Phrase bank use these
JobB2 · safeC1 · upgrade

Name the frameThe writer uses emotive words such as …The writer relies on emotive language such as …
Check the angleThe extract does not mention …The omission of … narrows the picture considerably.
Lamp and mistNo source is given for …The claim that … is presented as certain, although the evidence is disputed.

Common traps

✓ The author writes very emotionally / uses emotive language.

✓ According to the author, … / In the author’s opinion, …
✗ Extract B is more objective than other.
✓ Extract B is more objective than the other one.

Be the examiner

Examiners use four criteria. Use them to mark two students’ work, then apply them to your own analysis.

CriterionA C1 objectivity analysis …
T · Taskanswers the exact question and keeps one clear verdict from the glass to the fair conclusion
O · Organisationhas one point per sentence (verdict → glass → frame → angle → lamp + mist → conclusion) and links ideas with more than Firstly / Secondly
V · Vocabularyuses precise topic words and collocations in an academic tone
G · Grammaruses a range of structures with few errors; in this stop: cohesion: reference, substitution and ellipsis (it, the earliest ones, many do not, if so)

Score each criterion: 1 = not yet · 2 = almost · 3 = yes

Two students wrote a short analysis of Extract A (The Gift of Samarkand). Mark both.

Student A
Extract A is less objective than Extract B. Extract A gives some facts, for example the Battle of Talas in 751. But the writer writes very emotional about our ancestors and uses words like “brave” and “genius”. Extract A gives many informations, but Extract A does not give any sources. Some historians accept the prisoners story, but many not, and Extract A does not say this. In this text is written that paper was the greatest gift. So Extract A is bad and Extract B is good.
Student B
Extract A is largely celebratory rather than objective. Its factual core — that Samarkand became famous for its paper — can be checked, but the writer surrounds it with emotive language such as “brave”, “jealously” and “genius”. The omission of the historians’ debate about Talas narrows the picture, and claims such as “Everyone knows” are presented as certain without a source. Overall, it is useful as an example of pride in the past rather than as a neutral account.

Which criterion shows the biggest difference between A and B? Why?

Read like a detective

17 MIN

Do not start at the beginning. First look only at the cover and the contents of this report. A report is organised so that readers can go straight to the section they need.

The Campus Plate: How Students Eat

A survey report by the Student Health Committee of Caravan University (a fictional university) · written for this book · about 500 words · All numbers in this report are invented example data for practice.

Contents

Summary1
1  Introduction1
2  Method2
3  Findings2
    3.1 Breakfast2
    3.2 Fruit and vegetables3
    3.3 Sugary drinks3
4  Discussion4
5  Recommendations4
Appendix: the questionnaire5

Predict before you read

Look only at the contents. Which section will tell you …

a) how many students took part?
b) what the committee wants to change?
c) the main results in five lines?
d) why the results may be limited?
e) the exact questions students saw?

SummaryThis report presents the results of a survey on the eating habits of students at Caravan University. The survey found that many students skip breakfast, eat less fruit and vegetables than recommended, and buy more sugary drinks during examination periods. The report recommends three low-cost changes to the campus food environment.

1Introduction. Good nutrition supports concentration, mood and long-term health. International health organisations advise people to eat plenty of fruit and vegetables — often expressed as at least five portions a day — and to limit their sugar intake. University life, however, often changes the way young people eat: many students live away from home for the first time, have little money and study late at night. The aim of this survey was to find out how students at Caravan University eat and to suggest practical improvements.

2Method. An online questionnaire with 15 questions was sent to all students in October. It was completed by 600 respondents from all four years of study. Students recorded what they ate and drank during one typical week. In addition, the canteen provided monthly sales figures for sugary drinks for one academic year. Because the results are self-reported, they may be less accurate than direct observation, and students who care about healthy eating may have been more likely to take part.

Glossary: self-reported — given by the people themselves, not checked · direct observation — watching and counting what really happens · dormitory — a student hostel (yotoqxona) · grab-and-go — food you can take quickly and eat on the way

Öqiş va yozuv amaliyotiModule 3 · Practical class 26
3

Findings, figures and the way forward

CONTINUED

3 · Findings

3.1Breakfast. As Table 1 shows, the proportion of students who eat breakfast every day falls steadily from the first to the fourth year of study, from 62% to 41%. The most common reasons for skipping breakfast were “no time” and “not hungry in the morning”.

3.2Fruit and vegetables. On average, respondents ate 2.4 portions of fruit and vegetables a day, less than half of the recommended amount. Intake was slightly lower in the senior years. Students who lived with their families ate more than students in dormitories (3.1 compared with 1.9 portions a day).

Table 1. Eating habits by year of study (invented data)

YearEat breakfast dailyFruit & veg portions a dayCanteen 3+ times a week
1st62%2.748%
2nd55%2.552%
3rd48%2.357%
4th41%2.161%

n = 600 respondents (invented example)

Figure 1. Sugary drinks sold in the canteen, per student per week (invented data)

3.3Sugary drinks. Figure 1 shows canteen sales of sugary drinks per student per week across one academic year. Sales rose gradually from September to December and then peaked sharply in January, during the winter examination session, at 2.9 drinks per student per week. They fell steeply in February, remained stable in March and April, and rose again in May and June, reaching 2.6 in June, the summer examination period.

4Discussion. The findings suggest that eating habits become less healthy as students move through university and during stressful periods. The fall in breakfast eating may be linked to longer study hours in the senior years. The peaks in sugary drink sales coincide with examinations, which suggests that students use these drinks for quick energy. However, the survey cannot show cause and effect, and the sample may not represent all students.

5Recommendations. The committee recommends that the university (1) opens a “grab-and-go” breakfast stand near the main lecture hall from 8:00 to 10:00; (2) offers a free piece of fruit with every canteen lunch during examination sessions; and (3) places free drinking-water stations next to vending machines, with simple information on sugar content.

Jigsaw option. Expert groups: A — Summary + Introduction + Method; B — Findings + Table 1 + Figure 1; C — Discussion + Recommendations. Each group writes three questions that its part can answer. In mixed groups, the others must say which section to open before anyone gives the answer.
Talk after reading: Which recommendation would work best at your university? Why? And why does a careful report never say “prove”?

The data toolkit rule
MovementVerb (past)Noun+ how much / how fast
↗ uprise (rose) · increase · climb · growa rise · an increasesharply · steeply · dramatically (big, fast)
gradually · steadily (slow, regular)

Three rules

  • rise has no object: Sales rose ✓ · Sales raised ✗. raise needs one: The canteen raised its prices.
  • The number / proportion of students is … (singular verb) · A number of students are …
  • Verb + adverb, adjective + noun: sales fell sharply = a sharp fall in sales.

Level up: comparing and interpreting data

At C1 you do more than say that numbers go up or down. You compare them precisely, you round them honestly, and you say carefully what they may — and may not — mean.

Precise comparison

Approximation

Cautious result
a link, not a proof		coincide with · may be linked to · which suggests thatThe peaks coincide with the exams, which suggests that students drink them for energy.
Nominalisation
verb → noun phrase		rise → a sharp rise · fall → a steady fall · consume → consumptionSales fell steeply in February. → There was a steep fall in sales in February.

3. 62% of first-years eat breakfast every day. (just over three fifths)
4. Drink sales are high in exam months. Maybe students use them for energy. (coincide with … which suggests)
5. Students ate 2.4 portions, but five are recommended. (less than half of)

Remember from Stop 19: do not over-hedge

✗ Sales may possibly have perhaps risen a little bit in January, maybe.
✓ Sales rose sharply in January, which suggests a link with exams.  — report the numbers firmly; hedge only what they mean.

The head of the canteen sends a question. Watch how a student uses the logbook to answer it in three minutes — without reading the whole report.

Question: “Should we stop selling sugary drinks during exam sessions? What does the report say?”
1 · Keywords
The question is about sugary drinks, exam sessions and what to do. So I need numbers and a recommendation.
2 · Contents
“Sugary drinks” → 3.3. “What to do” → 5 Recommendations. A chart is probably in 3.3. I can skip 3.1 and 3.2.
3 · Jump + look
Figure 1: two shaded bars say “exams” — January and June. The line is highest there: 2.9 and 2.6.
4 · Read closely
3.3 confirms the peaks. Section 4 warns: the survey cannot show cause and effect. Section 5 does not say “stop selling” — it suggests water stations and sugar information.
5 · The note
According to Section 3.3 and Figure 1, sales of sugary drinks rose sharply and peaked in the two exam months, January (2.9 per student per week) and June (2.6). However, the report does not recommend a ban. Instead, Section 5 suggests free water stations next to the vending machines and clear information on sugar content. The committee also notes that the survey cannot prove that exams cause the rise (Section 4). (All figures are invented example data.)

Read like a detective

17 MIN

Before you read: navigate by the stars

Read only the title and the five headings. What will each section say? Write a short prediction.

HeadingMy prediction: this section will …Right?
1 Beyond copy and paste
2 Recycling yourself
3 The machine in the room
4 The missing mark
5 Looking ahead

Borrowed Words, Broken Trust

Plagiarism in the age of AI · an article written for this book · about 630 words · ★ = stop and predict

AScience runs on trust. When researchers publish a result, other scientists build on it, because nobody can repeat every experiment. This is why research ethics treats three kinds of misconduct as especially serious: fabrication (inventing data), falsification (changing data) and plagiarism (presenting others’ work as your own). The first two damage the facts; plagiarism damages the record of who discovered what. And in the age of copy-paste and artificial intelligence, it is taking new forms. ★1

B1 · Beyond copy and paste. Most students know that copying a paragraph word for word without quotation marks is plagiarism. Fewer recognise patchwriting: taking a source sentence and changing a few words — a synonym here, a different word order there — while keeping its structure and ideas. Patchwriting often comes from good intentions; many writers believe that changing words is the same as paraphrasing. A true paraphrase, however, begins with understanding: you close the source, explain the idea in your own words and structure, and then cite it. Because patchwriting is often a stage in learning to write, many teachers treat it as a reason for teaching rather than for punishment. In a published article, however, it is not acceptable.

C2 · Recycling yourself. Can you plagiarise yourself? Many universities say yes. ★2 Self-plagiarism means submitting the same work, or large parts of it, for a second assignment or publication without saying so. Imagine a student who hands in an essay from her first year again in her third year, as if it were new. The ideas are her own, but the teacher who gives the mark is misled about what is new. In research, reusing some text from an earlier paper can be acceptable when it is clearly disclosed; hiding it is not.

Öqiş va yozuv amaliyotiModule 3 · Practical class 27
3

Following the stars

CONTINUED

D3 · The machine in the room. Generative AI tools can now produce fluent paragraphs in seconds. Is text written by a machine plagiarism? Policies differ between universities and journals, and they are changing quickly. A common principle is emerging, however: if you present text produced by an AI tool as your own writing without disclosing it, you deceive the reader about who did the work. AI tools also create a second problem. ★3 They can produce references that look real but do not exist. A student who copies such a reference into an essay may cite an article that nobody ever wrote. For this reason, many institutions now ask writers to state clearly whether and how they used AI, and to check every source themselves.

E4 · The missing mark. Not all plagiarism is deliberate. A writer may take careful notes from a book, forget to record the source and later use the idea as if it were their own. Others cite a source in the text but forget the reference list, or copy exact words without quotation marks. These are failures of method rather than of honesty, but for the reader the result is the same: the original author’s mark has disappeared. Simple habits — recording the source with every note, adding quotation marks immediately, checking every citation before submission — prevent most of these problems.

F5 · Looking ahead. What will happen next? ★4 Prediction is risky, but some trends are already visible. Detection software will probably become more sophisticated, yet it is unlikely to solve the problem on its own, because AI-generated text is difficult to identify reliably. Many educators therefore expect assessment to change: more writing in class, more oral discussion of written work and more attention to drafts and notes. It is also likely that universities will teach students to use AI openly instead of simply banning it. One thing is unlikely to change: readers will continue to need to know whose words and ideas they are reading. Without that knowledge, the trust that science runs on cannot survive.

How sure? rule
CertaintyFormExample
▮▮▮▮ certainwill · will definitely · is certain toReaders will continue to need sources.
▮▮▮ probablewill probably · is likely to · may wellSoftware will probably improve.
▮▮ possiblemay · might · couldExams may move into the classroom.
▮ improbableis unlikely to · probably won’tIt is unlikely to solve the problem.
👁 evidence nowbe going toNo sources at all: it is going to fail.
⏳ at a future timewill be + -ing · will have + past participleWe will be using AI. · Rules will have changed.
📣 reportingX predict(s) that … will · X expect(s) Y to · is expected toThey expect exams to change.

Three rules

  • likely is an adjective: is likely to change ✓ · will likely to change ✗
  • expect + object + to: expect assessment to change ✓ · expect that assessment changing ✗
  • No present simple for predictions: AI will replace some tasks ✓ · In future AI replaces ✗

exact certainty		may well · there is every chance that · it seems improbable thatDetectors may well improve, yet it seems improbable that they will solve the problem alone.
Nominalisation
verb or adjective → noun		disclose → disclosure · detect → detection · rely → relianceStudents disclose AI use. → The disclosure of AI use is now expected.
Stance adverbs
your attitude		rightly · arguably · understandably · worryinglyWorryingly, some invented references look entirely authentic.

Phrase bank use these
JobB2 · safeC1 · upgrade
Give the verdictThe paragraph uses its sources only partly honestly.On the whole, the paragraph gives credit where it is due, except in …

Be the examiner

7 MIN

Examiners use four criteria. Learn them by marking someone else’s work first — then use them on your own source-use check.

CriterionA C1 source-use check …
T · Taskanswers the exact question: checks every borrowed idea against its source and keeps one clear verdict to the end
O · Organisationhas one point per sentence (verdict → each problem with evidence → likely result) and links ideas with more than Firstly / Secondly
V · Vocabularyuses precise topic words and collocations in an academic tone
G · Grammaruses a range of structures with few errors; in this stop: reporting and careful prediction (Rahimov (2025) warns that …, is likely to, will probably)

Score each criterion: 1 = not yet · 2 = almost · 3 = yes

Two students checked Dilnoza’s paragraph (Build it, Level 1) against its two sources. Mark both.

Student A
Dilnoza’s paragraph is not very honest. In sentence 2 she copied Yusupova and changed some words, so it is a copy. Sentence 3 is also from Rahimov, but she did not write his name. Sentence 5 is very strange, because the AI wrote it and she did not tell. Sentences 1 and 4 are her own, so they are OK. In future the teacher will likely to give her a bad mark, because this is stealing.
Student B
Dilnoza’s paragraph uses its sources only partly honestly. Sentence 2 is patchwriting: it keeps the structure of Yusupova’s sentence (2024, p. 18) and merely swaps four words, yet it gives no citation. Sentence 3 attributes nothing to Rahimov (2025), although the words “invent references that look authentic” come from his p. 7. Sentence 5 was produced by a chatbot, and this is not disclosed. Only sentences 1 and 4 are clearly her own. Unless these marks are restored, the paragraph is likely to be treated as plagiarism, even if the problems are accidental.

Read like a detective

17 MIN

Before you read: skim the three headings only. Which section will answer the question “Do people earn more because they move to the city?” Tick one.   1   2   3

Pushed, Pulled and Linked: Why Cities Grow

A textbook extract · Human geography · about 620 words · B2–C1 · written for this book

ATwo centuries ago, most people in the world lived in villages and worked on the land. Today, more than half of humanity lives in towns and cities, and the share is still rising. This shift, known as urbanisation, is one of the defining changes of the modern era. Urban growth results partly from births in the cities themselves and partly from migration from the countryside. Explaining it, however, is harder than it looks. Many trends appear together, and the challenge for researchers — and for readers — is to separate what causes urban growth from what merely accompanies it.

1 · Causes: the push and the pull

BGeographers often describe migration in terms of push and pull factors. Push factors drive people away from their home area: a shortage of land, low farm incomes, drought, or a lack of services such as hospitals and good schools. Pull factors attract them to the city: jobs, higher wages, universities and the hope of a more comfortable life. In practice, the two usually work together. A young farmer is unlikely to leave because of one bad harvest, but a series of poor harvests, combined with news of well-paid building work in the capital, may trigger a decision to move.

CThe causes are not only economic. Improvements in transport and communication have made moving far easier than it once was. A bus ticket and a mobile phone allow a migrant to stay in touch with family, find work through relatives and return home for weddings and holidays. Networks of earlier migrants therefore play an important role: people tend to move to places where friends or relatives have already settled, so each wave of migration helps to produce the next.

2 · Consequences for the city and the village

DThe effects of urbanisation can be seen at both ends of the journey. In the city, rapid growth often leads to heavy pressure on infrastructure. When the population rises faster than new housing can be built, rents increase, and new arrivals may be forced to settle on the outskirts, often in areas with poor roads and an unreliable water supply. Longer journeys to work, in turn, contribute to traffic congestion and air pollution. A single cause can thus set off a whole chain of effects.

EIn rural areas, the consequences are more mixed. Remittances — money sent home by migrants — can pay for new houses, education and small businesses, and in many villages of Central Asia they have become an important part of family income. At the same time, the departure of so many young people can leave behind an ageing population, and some farms struggle due to a shortage of workers.

Paragraph F changes direction. Which words signal this?
Öqiş va yozuv amaliyotiModule 3 · Practical class 28
3

Read like a detective

CONTINUED

3 · Cause or association?

FNot every link between two trends, however, is a causal one. Researchers have observed, for example, that moving to a city is often linked to higher income: migrants tend to earn more than relatives who stay behind. It is tempting to conclude that the city itself causes the higher income. Yet migrants are not a random group. They are often younger, healthier and better educated than average, and these qualities are likely to raise income wherever a person lives. In such cases, migration and higher income are associated with each other, but the city may be only part of the explanation.

GSometimes the direction of the link is unclear as well. Large cities are home to more universities, but this does not necessarily mean that universities make cities grow; growing cities may equally attract new universities. Careful readers therefore ask three questions whenever a text connects two things. Does one really lead to the other? Could a third factor explain both? And which way does the influence flow? Answering them is the first step towards reading — and writing — about cause and effect with precision.

Jigsaw option. Group A: A–C (causes) · Group B: D–E (consequences) · Group C: F–G (association). Draw your part as an ariq on a card and teach it to a new group in 60 seconds.
Talk after reading: Think of someone who moved to a city or abroad. Which push factor and which pull factor moved them? Was there a hidden source too?

Language toolkit: cause and effect

10 MIN

Cause–effect language has a direction and a strength. Get either wrong and you misreport the text.

Notice find it

Find these sentences in the text and complete them.

1. (A) Urban growth partly from births in the cities themselves …

2. (D) In the city, rapid growth often heavy pressure on infrastructure.

3. (D) Longer journeys to work, in turn, traffic congestion and air pollution.

4. (F) … moving to a city is often higher income …

5. (E) … some farms struggle a shortage of workers.

Direction and strength rule
JobLanguageExample
CAUSE → EFFECTlead to · result in · cause · triggerDrought leads to migration.
EFFECT ← CAUSEresult from · be caused by · stem fromMigration results from drought.
one of many causescontribute to · play a role inTraffic contributes to pollution.
only togetherbe linked to · be associated with · correlate withMigration is linked to income.
link two sentencesas a result · therefore · consequently · thusRents rose. As a result, …

Three rules

  • Mind the direction: cause results in effect · effect results from cause.
  • because + clause (because rents rose) · because of / due to + noun (due to high rents)
  • Match the evidence: causes > contributes to > is linked to. Not sure? Go weaker.
Fix it correct
Broken sentenceFixed sentence
1. Migration is resulted from low wages.
2. Because of rents rose, families moved out.
3. The drought caused to many families leave.
4. Migration effects the life of the village.
5. Low wages result from migration. (wages = cause)

Level up: precise cause and effect

CONTINUED

At C1 you name causes precisely — often as nouns — and you claim exactly as much as the evidence allows: no more, no less.

ToolPhrasesExample
Causal verbs
more precise than cause		give rise to · stem from · bring about · fuel · exacerbateRapid growth has given rise to new suburbs.
Nominalised causes
the cause as a noun		rise → the rise in · arrive → the arrival of · leave → the departure ofRents rose, so families moved. → The rise in rents pushed families out.
Careful causality
one of several causes		may partly account for · is likely to have contributed to · appears to stem fromBetter roads may partly account for the return of some migrants.
Association
a link, not proof		is closely associated with · a confounding factor · cannot be attributed solely toHigher income cannot be attributed solely to the move.

Remember from Stop 19: do not over-hedge

✗ Traffic might possibly perhaps contribute in some way to some pollution.
✓ Traffic may contribute to air pollution.  — one hedge per claim is enough. When you report a text, keep the writer’s own hedge (often, may): add none, drop none.

The scholar’s tool: the ariq

10 MIN

For centuries, farmers in Central Asia have depended on the ariq, the irrigation channel. Water always comes from somewhere, and a green field does not prove that your channel watered it. A reader of cause and effect needs the same two habits.

Before you accept that A causes B, check the source, the limits (gates) and any hidden third factor.

Part of the ariqIn the textAsk yourselfSignal words
Headwaterthe causeWhere does it all start?because of · due to · results from
Main channelthe linkHow does A produce B?leads to · as a result · therefore
Branchesmany effectsWhat else does it water?also · at the same time
Chain of fieldseffect → new causeWhat happens next?in turn · this then · which
Sluice gateconditions and limitsWhen? For whom?when · if · in some cases · often
Hidden sourcea link, not proofA third factor? Which way?is linked to · tends to
Compare it think
Scholar’s toolThe question it answers
Sieve (Stop 17)What are the main points? What can I let fall through?
Compass (Stop 20)Where is the writer going? What is the argument?
Ariq (Stop 28)Why did it happen? Is it a real cause — or only company?

Student A

Often and may limit even these claims. Paragraph F, by contrast, treats the link between migration and higher income only as an association, since the migrants’ age, health and education may be a confounding factor. G adds that the direction of a link can be unclear. Overall, each claim matches the evidence.

Read like a detective

17 MIN

Before you read: a report on a problem usually gives the problem first and the verdict last. Skim the headings. In which section will you find the writer’s recommendation?   1   2   3

Prescribing Clean Power: Central Asia’s Energy Challenge

A policy report extract · Energy studies · about 610 words · B2–C1 · written for this book

1 · The patient: a system under strain

AAcross Central Asia, the demand for electricity is rising fast. Populations are growing, cities are expanding and households own more appliances than ever before. For decades, most of this demand has been met by power stations that burn natural gas or coal and, in the mountainous parts of the region, by large hydropower dams. This system helped the region’s economies to develop. Today, however, it is showing clear signs of strain.

BThe symptoms are familiar to many families. In cold winters, demand reaches its peak exactly when gas is also needed for heating, and some districts experience shortages and power cuts. Much of the grid was built decades ago, so a considerable share of electricity is lost before it reaches homes. Burning fossil fuels also releases emissions that pollute city air and contribute to climate change. Finally, there is an economic cost: gas that is burned wastefully at home cannot be sold or used elsewhere. In short, the problem is not simply a lack of power, but a combination of high demand, old infrastructure and a heavy dependence on fossil fuels.

2 · Three treatments

CThe most visible response has been solar power. The region enjoys a large number of sunny days each year, and the price of solar panels has fallen sharply over the past decade. Large solar plants have been built in several countries of the region, and smaller panels are appearing on the roofs of schools and homes. Supporters describe solar energy as the obvious answer for a sunny region: it produces no emissions while it operates, and a plant can be built relatively quickly. Wind farms, built in open steppe areas where strong winds are common, offer a similar benefit.

DCritics point out, however, that both sources share a serious drawback: they are intermittent. The sun does not shine at night, and the wind does not always blow when power is needed. Solar output is also lowest in winter, the very season when demand is highest. To be reliable, these sources need storage, such as large batteries, or a grid that can switch quickly to other sources. Storage technology is improving, but at present it remains expensive.

EA second response is to make better use of hydropower. Dams can produce large amounts of electricity without emissions and, unlike solar panels, they can raise or reduce output within minutes. Yet hydropower has limitations of its own. Building a new dam is costly and slow, and the region’s great rivers cross national borders: water stored for electricity in winter is water that farmers downstream may need for irrigation in summer. Any expansion therefore requires close cooperation between neighbouring countries.

Who is speaking in C and D: the writer — or someone else?
Öqiş va yozuv amaliyotiModule 3 · Practical class 29
3

Read like a detective

CONTINUED

FA third, less glamorous treatment is to use less energy in the first place. Insulating walls and roofs, replacing old windows and installing modern heating systems can considerably reduce the energy a building needs, and repairing old power lines cuts losses in the grid. Such measures rarely make headlines, but many experts regard them as the most cost-effective first step.

3 · The verdict

GWhich treatment, then, should be prescribed? Judged by three questions — is it effective, is it feasible, and what are its side effects? — no single option is a cure. Solar and wind are effective at cutting emissions but cannot yet solve the winter peak on their own. Hydropower is flexible but depends on shared rivers. Efficiency is cheap and quick, yet it reduces demand rather than creating new supply. On balance, the most promising strategy appears to be a combination: efficiency first, renewables second, and hydropower and storage to keep the system stable. Like a good physician, policymakers will also need follow-up visits, measuring the results and adjusting the treatment as the patient changes.

Jigsaw option. Group A: A–B (diagnosis) · Group B: C–E (treatments) · Group C: F–G (cheapest cure + verdict). Each group fills its part of the tabib’s chart and reports to a new group in 60 seconds.
Talk after reading: Which treatment would you prescribe first for your own town? Why? Which side effect would you watch for?

The scholar’s tool: the tabib

10 MIN

Ibn Sino (Avicenna), born near Bukhara more than a thousand years ago, is remembered as one of the great tabibs (physicians) of history. His Canon of Medicine was studied by doctors in Asia and Europe for centuries. A good tabib works in order: diagnosis → treatment → evaluation. So does a good reader of problem–solution texts: you read the patient’s file and fill in the tabib’s chart.

A report evaluates each solution, including its drawbacks; a text that only praises a solution is closer to an advert.

The tabibIn the textAsk yourselfSignal words
Hears the storysituationWhat is the background?currently · in recent years
DiagnosisproblemWhat is wrong? Who suffers?challenge · strain · shortage
PrescriptionresponsesWhat was tried?one response · a measure
Side effectsdrawbacksWhat does it cost us?however · yet · a drawback
Follow-up visitevaluationDid it work? Which is best?effective · feasible · on balance
Compare it think
ToolWhat it does
Bridge (Stop 11)You built a problem–solution essay: problem bank → pillars → result bank.
Ariq (Stop 28)You read for causes: why did it happen?
Tabib (Stop 29)You read for cures: what is wrong, what helps — and does it really work?

From Cocoon to Atlas: A Process and a Case

A textbook extract · about 560 words (Part 1 ≈ 310 · Part 2 ≈ 250) · B2–C1 · written for this book

Part 1 · The process: how ikat silk is made

AMargilan, in the Fergana Valley, has been famous for its silk for centuries, and its ikat fabrics, atlas and adras, have become symbols of Uzbek craft. Atlas is woven entirely from silk, while adras combines silk with cotton. Producing them is a long process with many stages, and each stage depends on the one before it. A mistake made early cannot be corrected later.

BThe process begins with the silkworm, which, despite its name, is the caterpillar of a moth. For about a month, the worms are fed on fresh mulberry leaves and grow quickly. When they are fully grown, each one spins a cocoon around itself from a single, remarkably long thread. Before the moths can break out and damage the thread, the cocoons are collected and treated with heat.

CNext, the cocoons are soaked in hot water, which softens the natural gum that holds the thread together. The loose ends of several cocoons are then found and reeled together, so that many fine filaments become one stronger thread. After that, the raw silk is washed and wound onto frames, ready for the most famous stage of all.

DIn the ikat technique, known locally as abr, the pattern is created before the cloth is woven. First, the threads are stretched out side by side. Then the parts that must stay uncoloured are tied tightly, and the threads are dipped in dye. When the ties are removed, the first colour of the pattern appears. This is repeated for every colour, so a complex design may be tied and dyed many times. Finally, the threads are arranged on the loom and woven into cloth. Because the dye never stops exactly at the ties, the edges of the pattern look soft and blurred, like clouds — which is why the technique is called abr, the word for “cloud”.

Part 2 · The case: one family workshop

The Rahimov workshop is a fictional case, written for this book from the experience of many craft workshops.

EToday, the Rahimov family workshop in Margilan employs twenty weavers, and its scarves are bought by visitors from many countries. Its story, however, began long before the tourists arrived. In the 1980s, Karim Rahimov worked at a large silk factory, where cloth was produced by machines and few young people learned the old hand techniques.

Part 1 never says who does each step. Why not?
Öqiş va yozuv amaliyotiModule 3 · Practical class 30
3

Read like a detective

CONTINUED

FWhen the factory closed in the 1990s, Karim suddenly found himself without work. Instead of leaving the city, he set up two hand looms in his courtyard and asked his grandfather, who had learned abr dyeing as a boy, to teach him. For several years, the family barely survived. Subsequently, however, interest in traditional crafts began to grow, and by 2010 the workshop had trained a dozen apprentices.

GIn 2015, Karim’s daughter Nodira, who had studied economics in Tashkent, returned home and started to sell the scarves online. Within two years, sales had doubled. Meanwhile, the family opened its courtyard to visitors, who can now watch every stage of the process, and several former apprentices have opened workshops of their own. For Karim, the most important decision is still the first one: not to let the craft disappear.

HThe case illustrates a pattern seen in many craft towns. A skill that is almost lost survives in one family; it is then revived when old knowledge meets new markets and new technology. Read together, the two parts of this text show both sides of chronology: the fixed order of a process, and the changing order of a life.

Jigsaw option. Group A: A–B · Group B: C–D (the process) · Group C: E–H (the case). Each group draws its part as a row of the loom — one box per stage or event — and teaches it to a new group in 60 seconds.
Talk after reading: Which decision was the turning point for the workshop? Would the story work without it?

Language toolkit: tenses and time markers

10 MIN

A process text cares about what happens, not who does it — so it uses the passive. A case study tells what happened — so it uses past tenses, and had + V3 sends the reader further back.

Notice find it

Find these sentences in the text and complete them.

1. (B) For about a month, the worms on fresh mulberry leaves …

2. (C) , the cocoons in hot water …

3. (D) … the pattern before the cloth is woven.

4. (F) … by 2010 the workshop a dozen apprentices.

5. (G) , the family opened its courtyard to visitors …

Two kinds of time rule
Text typeFormExample
process (how)present simple passive: is / are + V3The threads are dyed.
case (what happened)past simpleKarim set up two looms.
an earlier pastpast perfect: had + V3His grandfather had learned abr.
start → endFirst · Next · Then · After that · FinallyFinally, the cloth is woven.
step + stepOnce / When + clause · MeanwhileOnce the ties are removed, …

Three rules

  • Passive = be + V3: are fed ✓ · are feed ✗ · weave → wove → woven (weaved)
  • An earlier past = had + V3: by 2010 the workshop had trained … ✓ · by 2010 … trained ✗
  • A finished time = past simple: in the 1990s the factory closed ✓ · has closed ✗
Fix it correct
Broken sentenceFixed sentence
1. The cocoons is soaked in hot water.
2. The silk was weaved by hand.
3. By 2010 the workshop trained a dozen apprentices.
4. Karim’s grandfather has learned abr long before the factory closed.
5. The old factory has closed in the 1990s.
☆Which came first? tick it

Tick the event that happened first.

1. By the time Nodira returned, the workshop had trained a dozen apprentices.  return training

2. Karim set up two looms after the factory had closed.  looms closure

Level up: read a packed sequence

CONTINUED

C1 writers pack two steps or events into one sentence, so the word order no longer shows the time order. Learn to unpack these structures when you read.

ToolPhrasesExample → what happens first
Reduced clauses
two steps in one		Once dried, … · After being soaked, … · Having been dyed, …Once dried, the threads are wound onto frames. → 1 dried · 2 wound
Formal sequencers
exact order		Prior to … · Upon + -ing · Subsequently · ThereafterPrior to weaving, the threads are dyed. → 1 dyed · 2 woven
Nominalisation
a step as a noun		remove → removal · produce → production · dye → dyeingAfter the removal of the ties, a colour appears. → 1 ties removed · 2 colour
Flashback signals
an earlier past		had + V3 · by then · by the time … · long beforeBy the time Nodira returned, the workshop had trained a dozen apprentices. → 1 trained · 2 returned

Remember from Stop 19: do not over-hedge

✗ The threads may perhaps possibly be dyed at some point.
✓ The threads are then dyed.  — a process step or a dated event is a fact: when you retell it, add no hedge.

The scholar’s tool: the silk loom

10 MIN

On a hand loom, nothing happens out of order. The warp is stretched first, the pattern is dyed into it before weaving, and the cloth grows one row at a time. Chronological texts — processes and case studies — are woven in the same way.

Stretch the warp first: put every stage or event on the timeline, then see where the text jumps.

Part of the loomIn the textAsk yourselfSignal words
Warpthe timelineWhat is the backbone?in the 1990s · by 2010
ShuttlesequencersWhat comes next?first · next · then · after that
Rowsone stage or eventWhere does a stage end?once · when · as soon as
Abr patternthe overviewHow many stages or periods?The process has four stages.
Cloth rollthe result, todayWhere does it end?finally · today · since then
Row out of orderflashback in a caseDid this happen earlier?had + V3 · long before
Compare it think
ToolWhat it shows
Caravan road (Stop 14)You wrote a story: departure → obstacle → turning point → arrival.
Ariq (Stop 28)Why did it happen? (cause → effect)
Tabib (Stop 29)What is wrong, and what helps? (problem → solution → evaluation)
Silk loom (Stop 30)In what order did it happen, or is it done? (stage → stage → result)

Process (P) or case study (C)? Write P or C.

In 1998, a hand loom was set up in a courtyard.
The threads are washed and wound onto frames.
Two years later, sales had doubled.
Once the ties are removed, a colour appears.

Walk along the loom

A short case study, written for this book (Dilfuza and her studio are fictional). It is told out of order. A student began a text order vs time order table for it.

The case
(1) Today, Dilfuza’s suzani studio in Nurata employs eight embroiderers, and its cushions are sold in three cities. (2) Dilfuza had learned embroidery from her mother as a girl, but as an adult she had trained as a nurse and had worked in a hospital for six years. (3) In 2015 she lost her job when the hospital closed, so she began to sell a few cushions at the local bazaar. (4) By 2018, orders had grown so much that she rented a small room and hired two neighbours. (5) Meanwhile, her younger brother built a simple website for the studio. (6) Since then, sales have risen every year, and last spring the studio opened a second room.

A tourist posted what the owner of a weaving workshop (fictional) told her — not in time order. Turn each post into a case-study sentence (past simple or had + V3 + a time marker). Then number the events 1–4 in the order they happened.

JobB2 · safeC1 · upgrade
Open the caseThe case begins in the present.The case opens with the outcome, then goes back to …
Go backBefore that, … had …Long before this, … had … · By then, …

Same timeAt the same time, …Meanwhile, …

Common traps

✗ In 2015 Nodira has returned home.
✓ In 2015 Nodira returned home.
✗ When Karim was born, his grandfather already learned abr.
✓ … had already learned abr.
✗ After, Karim set up two looms.
✓ After that, Karim set up two looms.
✗ Firstly … Secondly … Thirdly … (12 times)
✓ Vary it: First … By then … Two years later …

Then the factory closed. Then Karim set up looms. Then interest grew. Then the workshop trained a dozen apprentices.

LEVEL 2

Untangle a new case

A Second Life for Old Doors · a short case study · about 120 words · written for this book (Bahodir and his workshop are fictional)

Last year, a small woodcarving workshop in Kokand won a national design prize for a set of carved panels, although only a few years earlier it had almost closed. Its founder, Bahodir, had carved doors for local houses since the 1990s, but by 2016 most customers preferred cheap metal doors, and he had only one apprentice left. That year, a hotel in Khiva asked him to repair its old wooden gates. While he was working on them, he noticed that tourists photographed the carvings more than anything else. He then began to make small carved panels for visitors. Within three years, the panels had become the workshop’s main product, and four new apprentices had joined.

Event (text order)Clue (time marker · tense)Time order
The workshop won a national design prize.
The workshop almost closed.
Bahodir began to carve doors for local houses.
A hotel asked him to repair its gates.
The panels became the main product.

My note (about 40 words): Where does the flashback start, and which words signal it? Why does the writer open with the prize?

8

Be the examiner

7 MIN

Examiners use four criteria. Practise them on two reading notes first, then use them on your own.

CriterionA C1 reading note on a chronology …
T · Taskretells the events accurately in time order and explains how the text order differs
O · Organisationfollows a clear timeline (earliest → latest) and links events with time markers, not just then … then
V · Vocabularyuses precise topic words and time markers in an academic tone
G · Grammaruses a range of structures with few errors; in this stop: narrative tenses and time clauses (past simple, past perfect had + V3, by 2010, when / after / by the time …)

Score each criterion: 1 = not yet · 2 = almost · 3 = yes

Two students did the same task: In about 80 words, retell the Rahimov case (Part 2) in time order and say how the text order differs. Mark both.

Student A
The text starts with today: the workshop has twenty weavers. In the 1980s Karim has worked at a silk factory. When the factory closed, his grandfather already learned abr, so he teached Karim. Then Karim set up two looms, and by 2010 the workshop trained a dozen apprentices. In 2015 Nodira has returned and sold scarves online, and sales doubled. So the text order is different because it starts with today.
Student B
The case opens with the outcome, a workshop of twenty weavers, and then moves back to the 1980s, when Karim worked in a silk factory. The earliest event appears only later, as a flashback: his grandfather had learned abr dyeing as a boy. After the factory closed in the 1990s, Karim set up two looms, and by 2010 the workshop had trained a dozen apprentices. In 2015 Nodira returned and began selling online; within two years, sales had doubled.

Which criterion shows the biggest difference between A and B? Why?
